docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Ce guide s'appuie sur trois ensembles de sources, dans cet ordre d'autorité :

  1. La Bible en kisiei (BKG), norme de l'orthographe et de l'usage ;
  2. le manuel de Keita (Keita 1979) et ses annotations manuscrites, description de base de la grammaire ;
  3. la grammaire et le dictionnaire de Childs (Childs 1995, 2000), description du kissi du Sud, pour la comparaison.

La page Sources et norme explique ce choix.

  • Bibliographie : toutes les références citées ;
  • Archives : les documents conservés dans le dépôt ;
  • Outils : la liste des mots de la Bible, la concordance et les vérifications automatiques.

docs.title: Outils
docs.text: Les règles de ce guide sont dégagées des textes de la Bible en kisiei (BKG) à l'aide de quelques outils, disponibles dans le dossier tools/ du dépôt. Ils s'exécutent avec uv.

docs.title: Le texte de la Bible
docs.text:
tools/fetch_bible.py télécharge les chapitres de la Bible en kisiei depuis bible.com, lentement (environ un par seconde), dans un dossier local .cache/bible/ qui n'est pas versé dans le dépôt : le texte reste la propriété de l'Alliance Biblique en Guinée. Seule la liste des formes de mots est publiée.

uv run tools/fetch_bible.py --delay 1.0

docs.title: La liste des formes de mots
docs.text: tools/build_wordlist.py produit references/bible-bkg-wordforms.tsv : chaque forme de mot de la Bible (sans tenir compte des tons ni des majuscules), son nombre d'occurrences, ses graphies avec accents de ton et une première référence. La Bible complète (1 188 chapitres) compte environ 939 000 mots et près de 22 000 formes différentes.

docs.title: La concordance
docs.text:
tools/bible_concordance.py cherche dans le texte local un mot, une partie de mot ou un motif, et affiche chaque occurrence dans son contexte avec sa référence. C'est l'outil principal pour vérifier une règle :

uv run tools/bible_concordance.py -w "ndɔ(ɔ|a|lan|len)"

docs.title: Les vérifications automatiques
docs.text:
À chaque construction du site (mkdocs build --strict), un module (tools/kisiei_hooks.py) :

  • vérifie que chaque exemple kisiei marqué comme attesté figure dans la liste des formes de la Bible ; sinon, la construction échoue ;
  • transforme les citations (« (Keita 1979, p. 57) ») en liens vers la bibliographie et signale les clés inconnues ;
  • accepte aussi une abréviation entre doubles crochets (code du livre, chapitre et verset, par exemple GEN.1.3) pour une référence biblique, mais les pages écrivent les références comme de simples liens Markdown vers le verset sur bible.com ([Gn 1,3](https://www.bible.com/bible/1394/GEN.1.3.BKG)), lisibles aussi hors du site.

tools/check_i18n.py vérifie que chaque page existe en français et en anglais.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
This guide is for everyone who writes, corrects or teaches Kisiei: teachers, translators, literacy workers, authors. It answers two questions: how do you spell this word? and how does this construction work?

  • Introduction: the language, its regional varieties, the history of its writing and the sources of the guide.
  • Spelling: the alphabet, vowels, consonants, tones, word division and punctuation, with a table from the old to the new spelling.
  • Grammar: the noun and its classes, agreement, determiners, pronouns, the verb, invariable words and the sentence.
  • Reference: verb tables, word lists by topic, common phrases, a glossary and open questions.

docs.title: Kisiei — spelling and grammar
docs.text: A reference guide for writing and teaching Kisiei (Northern Kissi).

docs.title: The standard: the Kisiei Bible
docs.text: The spelling in this guide is that of the Kisiei Bible (Bii Bila) (BKG). It is the longest and most recent text published in the current spelling; when another source spells a word differently, the Bible's form is authoritative. The grammar is based on Sékou Sondo Keita's manual (1979), reread in the light of the Bible's usage: every rule from 1979 has been checked against the biblical text, and the examples are taken from it wherever possible.

docs.title: Reading the examples
docs.text:
Kisiei words are in italics and underlined. The colour of the underline shows where the form comes from (details appear when you hover over it):

Mark Meaning pɔmbɔɔ Attested The form occurs exactly as written in the Bible (apart from tones). cɛi lakoli Respelled A form from the 1979 manual respelled according to the current rules, but not found in the Bible. To be confirmed by a speaker. mbara kisi To check Uncertain form or meaning (hard-to-read handwritten note, isolated word…).

See How to read this guide for the other conventions.

Draft

This guide is a first complete version. The rules are drawn from two written sources; they still need to be reviewed by Kisiei speakers. Uncertain points are collected in the open questions.

docs.title: The principle
docs.text:
In Kisiei, the class of a noun is repeated on the words that accompany or replace it: subject pronouns, demonstratives, possessives, adjectives, relatives. This system is called the alliterative structure (Keita 1979, p. 121-122); Southern Kissi has the same agreement system, which affects pronouns, adjectives, possessives, demonstratives and small numbers (Childs 1995, p. 150). It is called alliterative because the same ending comes back like an echo through the sentence. The small words that carry this repetition are the class referents.

Lɛŋnden le va tulumasaa — “The earth (le) was without form” Gen 1:2: lɛŋnden belongs to the len class, and the subject pronoun that refers back to it is le.

Ɲumma bɛndu-bɛnduan ma va matoalaa — “The very great waters (ma) were…” Gen 1:2: a noun of the an class, taken up by ma.

kobilan la va belaŋɔmpum, lan la va… — “The cities (la) were sixty, those (lan la) were…” Deut 3:4: a plural in -lan, taken up by la and lan.

flowchart LR
    N["Noun of the <i>len</i> class<br><i>lɛŋnden</i> “earth, land”"]
    N --> S["Subject pronoun <i>le</i><br><i>Lɛŋnden le va tulumasaa</i>"]
    N --> O["Object pronoun <i>len</i>"]
    N --> D["Demonstrative <i>len</i><br><i>lɛŋnde len</i>"]
    N --> P["Possessive “his, her” <i>ndɔlen</i>"]
    N --> F["Final referent <i>-len, -nden</i>"]
    classDef noun stroke:#d07a2a,stroke-width:3px
    class N noun
One class, many words: the mark of the len class comes back on every word that refers to the noun (forms from the table below).

docs.title: Table of referents
docs.text:
The table brings together the forms described in 1979 (Keita 1979, p. 57-60, 85-86, 121) and checked in the Bible (BKG). The subject and object pronouns correspond, class by class, to those of Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 107).

Class Example Subject Object pronoun Near demonstrative Far demonstrative Possessive “his, her” Final referent o / a / ɔ sing. cuaa, yɔmndo o ndu hoo kon ndɔɔ -o, -ndo, -yo, -lo (fula-o) plural persons vannda, poaa a nda haa kan ndɔa -a, -nda i / e sing. sɔɛi, ciŋnde i ndi he ken ndɔɛi -e, -nde, -ye i / e plur. (-on) sɔɔn, pelon n mun mun mun ndɔn -on, -ndon an mɛnndan ma man man man ndɔan -an, -ndan len lɛŋnden, bollen le len len len ndɔlen -len, -nden lan diolan, kobilan la lan lan lan ndɔlan -lan, -ndan

Remarks:

  • The subject is the pronoun placed before the verb when the noun is not repeated, or just after the noun to take it up again (Lɛŋnden le va). In the o class, this resumptive pronoun is usually omitted (Mí Hala dimi aa), as in Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 108).
  • The demonstratives of the an, len and lan classes have the same form for “this” and “that”; it is the tone that distinguishes them (low for nearness, high for distance) (Keita 1979, p. 58). In Southern Kissi, the near demonstrative carries a falling tone and the far one a high tone, in all classes (Childs 1995, p. 110).
  • The 3rd-person possessive takes the ending of the class of the noun possessed, not of the possessor: kala ndɔ “his mother”, poaa ndɔa “his sons”, diola ndɔlan “his name”. See Possessives.

docs.title: Examples in the Bible
docs.text: Class Example Translation o cɛi kon that house Exod 40:19 i sɔɛi he this word Gen 9:17 i sɔɛi ken that word Gen 14:13 an mɛmma man these waters Gen 1:2 len bollen le dendu the head (le) has turned white 1 Sam 12:2 lan kobilan la va belaŋɔmpum the cities were sixty Deut 3:4 plural ɲɛm pangelen mun these lights Gen 1:14 an mɛmma diinun man the gathered waters Gen 1:10

docs.title: The final referent and the hyphen
docs.text:
When a noun phrase is completed by a relative clause, a complement or a proper noun, the class of the noun is taken up again at the end of the phrase by the referent, attached by a hyphen to the last word (see Word division):

  • kɔngɔ vesɛi fula-o “the dry land that appeared” Gen 1:10 (kɔngɔ, o class);
  • visia pɔmbɔa kela lɛŋ-nda “the small creatures that move on the ground” Gen 1:24 (visia, plural of persons/animals);
  • mɛmma co lebɛngu-an “the waters that are below” Gen 1:7 (mɛmma, an class);
  • sɔɛi Mɛlɛka dimul ndu-e “the word that the Lord had spoken to him” Gen 15:6 (sɔɛi, i class).

Rule

To write a pronoun, a demonstrative, a possessive or a referent correctly, you need to know the class of the noun and its number, then take the corresponding form from the table.

Note

The forms in the table marked as unattested and the exact distribution of referents for some classes remain to be confirmed; see the open questions.

docs.title: Grammar
docs.text:
This part describes the grammar of Kisiei as it emerges from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG), the standard of this guide, comparing it with the 1979 description (Keita 1979) and with the grammar of Southern Kissi (Childs 1995).

The central feature of the language is the system of noun classes: every noun belongs to a class, and the class is repeated on the words that go with it. That is why the grammar begins with the noun and agreement.

  1. The noun and agreement;
  2. Determiners and quantifiers;
  3. Pronouns;
  4. The verb;
  5. Invariable words;
  6. The sentence.

Each page gives the rule, examples taken from the Bible with their reference, and, in a box, the 1979 usage where it differs.

docs.title: Position and agreement
docs.text:
The qualifying adjective is placed after the noun. The noun takes its stem form and the adjective receives the class suffix of the noun (Keita 1979, p. 54-55) (Childs 1995, p. 125-126). The rules and examples below are taken from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG).

Class Example Meaning o pee bɛndoo great river Gen 15:18 o pee pɔmbɔɔ small river Gen 15:18 plural persons vanaa bɛndua chiefs, masters Gen 1:28 plural persons navaa kɛndɛa fine cows Gen 41:20 i duɲɛi bɛnduei great feast Lev 23:2 i hoeyii kɛndɛi pleasing smell Gen 8:21 an mɛmma bɛnduan great waters, flood Gen 6:17 len lɛŋnde kɛndɛlen good land Deut 8:7 len yinnde bɛndulen great fire Exod 19:18 lan peela bɛndulan / peela pɔmbɔlan large / small streams Exod 7:19 lan kobila bɛndulan great cities Gen 41:34 plur. in -on cieon bɛndon large villages Num 32:16

The noun is put into the stem form described on the Noun classes page: bare stem in the o class (pee bɛndoo), stem + class pronoun in the an, len and lan classes (mɛmma bɛnduan, lɛŋnde kɛndɛlen, kobila bɛndulan). The same order (noun + class pronoun + adjective + suffix) is described for Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 150).

docs.title: Forms of some common adjectives
docs.text:
The stem of the adjective stays the same; only the suffix changes. Its final vowel combines with the suffix, as in Southern Kissi, where bɛ̀ndù + -ó gives bɛ̀ndòó (Childs 1995, p. 201) (Bible: bɛndoo):

Meaning o plural persons i an len lan plur. -on big bɛndoo bɛndua bɛnduei bɛnduan bɛndulen bɛndulan bɛndon good, beautiful kɛndɔɔ kɛndɛa kɛndɛi kɛndɛan kɛndɛlen kɛndɛlan small pɔmbɔɔ pɔmbɔa pɔmbɔan pɔmbɔlen pɔmbɔlan bad vɔɔndo vɔɔnda

The empty cells correspond to forms not found in the Bible; they are built on the same pattern, with the status Respelled.

Adjectives proper form a closed class: dimensions, colours, age, basic qualities (Childs 1995, p. 126-127). Many other qualities are expressed by stative verbs or adjectives derived from verbs; see Stems and groups.

docs.title: The adjective used as a noun
docs.text: Preceded by the class pronoun, the adjective is used on its own, like a noun: o humbuo “the white one (the one that is white)”, ma tuuvan “the hot (liquid)” (Keita 1979, p. 55).

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text:
Intensity is expressed:

  • by the adverb taw “very, a lot” after the adjective or the stative verb: dɛnɛ kɛndɔɔ taw “a very great good” Gen 12:16, n naŋ taw “it was very good” Gen 1:31;
  • by reduplication of the adjective, written with a hyphen: bɛndu-bɛnduan “very great (waters)” Gen 1:2.

Intensive reduplication is also described in Southern Kissi (bɛ̀ndùbɛ́ndù “very big”) (Childs 1995, p. 126).

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Comparison is made with the verb hiow “surpass” (Keita 1979, p. 55-56):

  • Kɛwvo ndóò hiow visia yondoa … kɔlkalu vɔɔndo ni “The serpent surpassed all the wild animals in cunning” Gen 3:1;
  • pangele hiow vaa “the greater light” Gen 1:16.

Southern Kissi compares in the same way with the verb “surpass”; the superlative there is expressed as “surpass all” (Childs 1995, p. 283-285).

Spelling rules

  • The adjective is written separately from the noun: lɛŋnde kɛndɛlen, not lɛŋndekɛndɛlen.
  • The class suffix is written only once, on the adjective: pee bɛndoo, not peeo bɛndoo.
  • Fixed compounds are an exception and are written attached or with a hyphen; see Compound nouns.

docs.title: Demonstratives
docs.text: Demonstratives point to a being or a thing. Kisiei has two series of them: one for what is near (“this”), the other for what is far or already mentioned (“that”). Like the other determiners, they agree with the class of the noun (see Agreement).

docs.title: Table
docs.text: Class of the noun Near: adjective Near: pronoun Far Example (Bible) o / a / ɔ sing. ho hoo kon kobio ho “this city” Gen 18:24; kobi kon “that city” Gen 4:17 plural persons ha haa kan vannda ha “these people” Gen 7:1; vanaa kan “those people” Gen 10:5 i he hee ken pembei he “this mountain” Exod 3:12; pembii ken “that mountain” Gen 22:14 an man man man kooma man “this blood” Exod 12:13 len len len len paale len “that day” Gen 30:35 lan lan lan lan kobila lan “these cities” Gen 19:25 plural in -on / -n mun mun mun sɔɔn mun “these words, these things” Gen 22:1; ɲɛm mun “these things” Gen 21:14

docs.title: Form of the noun before the demonstrative
docs.text:
The texts of the Bible (BKG) confirm the rule described in 1979 (Keita 1979, p. 57):

  • with the near demonstrative, the noun keeps its full form: kobio ho, vannda ha, pembei he;
  • with the far demonstrative, the noun takes its stem form: kobi kon, vanaa kan.

Southern Kissi has the same distribution: the near demonstrative follows the full form of the noun, the far one follows the stem (accompanied by the class pronoun outside the o class) (Childs 1995, p. 110-111).

In the i class, the stem form before ken replaces -ei with -ii: pembei he / pembii ken “this/that mountain”, paangei he / paangii ken “this/that month” Exod 12:3 Gen 8:5.

In the an, len and lan classes, the noun is always in the stem form + class pronoun (mɛmma man, lɛŋnde len, kobila lan; see Noun classes). Near and far are distinguished there by tone (Keita 1979, p. 58), which the Bible does not mark. In Southern Kissi, the near demonstrative carries a falling tone and the far one a high tone (Childs 1995, p. 110).

Spelling rule

  • Near adjective: ho, ha, he (a single vowel): kobio ho.
  • Near pronoun, used on its own: hoo, haa, hee (double vowel): Hoo co “this one is…” Luke 23:38.
  • The demonstrative is always written separately from the noun.

docs.title: Uses of the pronoun
docs.text:
The demonstrative used on its own replaces a noun:

  • Hoo co masa Yuifia ni “This is the king of the Jews” Luke 23:38;
  • Le hee “because of this, that is why”, very frequent at the start of a sentence Gen 2:21;
  • O kon kɔɔli “after that” (o class), a narrative formula: O sɔɔn mun kɔɔli “after these events” Gen 22:1.

1979 usage

In 1979, ho and hoo are given as a single form, and tan, ten as variants of lan, len after l (Keita 1979, p. 57-58). The Bible distinguishes ho (adjective) and hoo (pronoun) and does not use tan, ten as demonstratives. The description of Southern Kissi also gives a single form for the adjective and the pronoun (hóò) (Childs 1995, p. 110).

docs.title: Indefinites
docs.text: Indefinites refer to beings and things in a vague way: “a certain”, “other”, “all”, “each”, “anyone”. Like the other determiners, they are placed after the noun (Keita 1979, p. 71-73). The forms below are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG).

docs.title: Invariable
docs.text:
Word Meaning Example (Bible) pum a certain, a Pee bɛndoo pum “a great river” Gen 2:10; Telen pum hiovɔɔ “some time passed” Gen 4:3 celen other, another po celen “another son” Gen 4:25; cuavaa celen “other children” Gen 5:4 tɔ̀a the others vanaa tɔ̀a “the other people” Gen 4:15 kpow all, whole o lɛŋnden kpow coo “on the whole earth” Gen 1:11; súúlan kpow “all kinds” Gen 1:21 kpede all (without exception) yowva kpede “all the birds” Gen 8:17 faw all, entirely visia bɛndua a à pɔmbɔa faw “the animals great and small, all of them” Gen 8:17

celen varies neither in class nor in number (po celen, cuavaa celen). pum corresponds to the Southern Kissi adjective pùm “some” (Childs 1995, p. 127).

docs.title: “Each”, “any”: X oo X
docs.text:
A repeated noun, linked by oo, means “each, every”:

  • bil oo bil “every plant”; yɔm oo yɔm “every tree” Gen 1:29;
  • Visi oo visi “each animal” Gen 2:19;
  • fonda oo fonda “everywhere, in every place” Gen 20:13.

The noun is in the stem form; oo is written separately. Several time nouns take a prefix i- and other nouns the class pronoun le-: idii oo idii “every morning” 2 Kgs 16:15, icɔl oo icɔl “every evening” 1 Kgs 17:6, ipaangu oo ipaangu “every month” 1 Kgs 5:28, lepola oo lepola “each tribe” Deut 1:23.

The same construction (the “distributive”) is described for Southern Kissi: a noun repeated around a particle ó, with the class pronoun prefixed outside the o class, and a prefix ì- before certain time nouns (Childs 1995, p. 197-198).

docs.title: “Someone, something”: reduplication
docs.text:
Reduplication with a hyphen forms the indefinites for persons and things:

  • vana-vana “someone, anyone”; with negation, “nobody”: vana-vana ve lasiɛmbu “nobody was ashamed” Gen 2:25;
  • ɲɛ-ɲɛ “something, anything”; with negation, “nothing”: ɲɛ-ɲɛ ve lecoo le “there was nothing on it” Gen 1:2.

docs.title: “The same, a single”: agreement
docs.text:
pilɛ “one” forms an indefinite that agrees with the class of the noun, in the sense of “the same, a single”:

Class Form Example o pilɔɔ baa pilɔɔ “in one place” Gen 1:9 i pilɛi dialii pilɛi “one flesh” Gen 2:24 len pilɛlen Paale pilɛlen “the same day” Gen 17:26 lan pilɛlan diomnda pilɛlan “the same words” Gen 11:1

In the 1979 description, this series is written pilöö, pilèi, pilèlen, pilèlan (Keita 1979, p. 71).

Spelling rules

  • Indefinites are written separately from the noun: po celen, yowva kpede.
  • Reduplicated indefinites take a hyphen: vana-vana, ɲɛ-ɲɛ.
  • X oo X is written as three words: visi oo visi.

1979 usage

The 1979 description also cites kèkè “any” and yööli “all” (Keita 1979, p. 71), which do not appear in the Bible; the Bible uses X oo X and kpow. These words remain to be checked with speakers. Southern Kissi has kɛ́kɛ̀ “any”, preceded by the class pronoun (ò-kɛ́kɛ̀ “anyone, anything”) (Childs 1995, p. 160).

docs.title: Determiners and quantifiers
docs.text:
Determiners are placed after the noun, which then takes its stem form; they carry the class suffix of the noun (see Agreement).

  • Adjectives;
  • Demonstratives: ho, kon, he, ken…;
  • Possessives: nuu, nɔmndo, ndɔɔ…;
  • Interrogatives: nɛ̀ɛ́, yɛɛ, kuɛɛ…;
  • Indefinites: pum, celen, kpow, X oo X…;
  • Numbers: cardinals, ordinals, agreement.

docs.title: Interrogatives
docs.text: The rules on this page are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG), compared with the 1979 description (Keita 1979, p. 64-69).

docs.title: Question words
docs.text:
Word Meaning Example (Bible) nɛ̀ɛ́ who? (subject) Nɛ̀ɛ́ cɔm yɛ nɔm “Who showed you…?” Gen 3:11 nɛ̀ɛ́-nɛ̀ who (is it)? Nɔm nɛ̀ɛ́-nɛ̀ “Who are you?” Gen 27:18 yɛɛ what? which? Dɛnɛ yɛɛ n tosa yɛ hoo “What have you done?” Gen 3:13 le yɛɛ why? Le yɛɛ n tambu yɛ kɔl “Why are you angry?” Gen 4:6 kuɛɛ where?; which? Kuɛɛ nɛ n co yɛ “Where are you?” Gen 3:9; Langbanɔ kuɛɛ co yɛ hoo “Who is this man?” Gen 24:65 vɛ̀ɛ̀ is it that…? how? Vɛ̀ɛ̀ o co kɛndɛ lon “Is he well?” Gen 29:6 bàà is it really…? bàà mà tɛɛmbuu nda “will you really destroy them?” Gen 18:24

The same words exist in Southern Kissi: kùɛ́ɛ́ “where”, nɛ̀ɛ́ “who”, yɛ̀ɛ́ “what”, wɛ̀ɛ́ “how, how much” (Childs 1995, p. 111, 264); the initial w there corresponds to the v of the Bible (vɛ̀ɛ̀).

docs.title: Content questions (who, what, where…)
docs.text:
1. The question word is placed at the start of the sentence, or just after the noun it determines (Dɛnɛ yɛɛ “what thing”, Langbanɔ kuɛɛ “which man”).
  2. It is often followed by the particle nɛ, which is optional and makes no notable difference in meaning (likewise in Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 144)): Kuɛɛ nɛ n co yɛ “Where are you?”, Yɛɛ nɛ kendu yɛ a Mɛlɛka “Is anything too hard for the Lord?” Gen 18:14. In Southern Kissi, this particle (-nɛ́) is optional and does not change the meaning (Childs 1995, p. 111, 265).
  3. The verb is followed by the particle yɛ, which closes the question: n co yɛ, n tosa yɛ. In the future, yɛ attaches to -nin: yɛnin (vɛ̀ɛ̀ ya sina yɛnin “how shall I know?” Gen 15:8).

The subject pronoun takes the form of the relative series: n “you (sing.)”, ya “I”, naa n “we”, niaa “you (plur.)” (Kuɛɛ nɛ n co yɛ “Where are you?”; kuɛɛ niaa fula yɛ “where do you come from?” Gen 29:4). See Relative clauses.

The question-final particle is already described in 1979 (yè, “a particle that appears after the verb”) (Keita 1979, p. 67). Southern Kissi has the same particle yɛ̀, placed after the conjugated verb; it is absent when the clause has no conjugated verb (Childs 1995, p. 111, 265).

docs.title: Yes/no questions
docs.text:
A yes/no question opens with vɛ̀ɛ̀: Vɛ̀ɛ̀ a yeema mì la kɔɛ niaa langbanɔɔ ho “Will you go with this man?” Gen 24:58. Without a question word, only the rising voice marks the question; in writing, the question mark is enough (Keita 1979, p. 69). In Southern Kissi, this is the general case: a yes/no question differs from a statement only by its rising intonation (Childs 1995, p. 264).

bàà introduces a question that expects a negative answer or expresses surprise Gen 20:4.

Spelling rules

  • Question words are written separately: le yɛɛ, Dɛnɛ yɛɛ.
  • nɛ̀ɛ́ and vɛ̀ɛ̀ carry their tone marks, as in the Bible; this distinguishes them from nɛɛ and vɛɛ.
  • The question ends with ? with no space before it; inside quotation marks: «Kuɛɛ nɛ n co yɛ?».

1979 usage

The 1979 description gives three interrogative adjectives (köè “which”, ngö “which” before the noun, nèènè “whose”) and three pronouns (nèè “who”, kuè “which one”, ngö) (Keita 1979, p. 64-67). The Bible uses nɛ̀ɛ́ “who”, kuɛɛ “where, which” and yɛɛ “what”; the forms köè and ngö do not appear there and remain to be checked with speakers.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text: The forms and rules on this page are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG), which contains a great many numbers (ages, censuses, dates). They are compared with the 1979 arithmetic lessons (Keita 1979, p. 16-63) and with the description of Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 112-114).

docs.title: From 1 to 10
docs.text:
1 pilɛ 6 ŋɔmpum 2 tiɔn 7 ŋɔmmɛw 3 yáá 8 ŋɔmaa 4 hiɔɔlu 9 ŋɔmahiɔɔlu 5 ŋuɛɛnu 10 tɔ́

The numbers from 6 to 9 are built on 5: ŋɔm- + 1, 2, 3, 4 (ŋɔmpum, ŋɔmmɛw, ŋɔmaa, ŋɔmahiɔɔlu).

docs.title: Tens, hundreds, thousands
docs.text:
20 bidiin 70 belaŋɔmmɛw 30 beleyaa 80 belaŋɔmaa 40 belehiɔɔlu 90 belaŋɔmahiɔɔlu 50 beleŋuɛɛnu 100 kɛmɛ 60 belaŋɔmpum 1000 vaa (plur. valan)

The words for 100 and 1000 are loanwords from Manding (Childs 1995, p. 112). The tens from 30 to 90 are formed with bele- / bela- + the unit. The hundreds are formed with le-: kɛmɛ lediin “200” Gen 11:19, kɛmɛ leyáá “300” Gen 5:22, kɛmɛ leŋɔmpum “600” Gen 7:6. Thousands are counted with the plural valan: vàálan tan ŋɔmmɛw a kɛmɛ leŋuɛɛnu “7,500” Num 3:22.

docs.title: Compound numbers
docs.text:
The parts of a compound number are linked by a “and”, from the largest to the smallest: kɛmɛ a beleyaa “130” Gen 5:3, bidiin a laŋɔmahiɔɔlu “29” Gen 11:24.

The last element takes a prefix agreeing with the class of the noun counted, as in Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 112-113):

Noun counted Prefix Example lan (vɔsilan “years”) la- vɔsilan kɛmɛ leŋɔmahiɔɔlu a tɔ́ a latiɔn “912 years” Gen 5:8 persons, animals à visia tɔ́ a à hiɔɔlu “14 animals” Gen 7:2 len (ordinal) le- paale bidiin a leŋɔmmɛwndɔle “the 27th day” Gen 8:14

Spelling rules

  • The elements of a compound number are written separately, linked by a: kɛmɛ a beleyaa.
  • The agreement prefix is written attached to the unit: latiɔn, laŋuɛɛnu; the prefix for persons à is written separately, with its tone.
  • In running text, large numbers may be written in figures, in brackets after the form in words, as the Bible does: “(7 500)”.

docs.title: Position of the number and agreement
docs.text:
The number is placed after the noun. From 2 upwards, it is often preceded by the class pronoun of the noun (object form; see Personal pronouns):

Class Example Meaning plural persons simlacia nda yáá three warriors 1 Chr 11:15 i plur. palɛi ndii yáá three days 1 Chr 12:40 plur. in -on Paangon mún yáá three months 1 Chr 13:14 an polan man yáá three rows 1 Kgs 6:36 lan kundala bɛndulan tan tiɔn two great (lights) Gen 1:6

Without a pronoun, the number follows the noun directly: kɔla palɛi yaa “a three days’ journey” Exod 3:18, vanaa yaa “three people”. The pronoun of the lan class takes the form tan after n (vàálan tan).

“Two” changes form according to the class of the noun counted: ŋiɔn for persons (poaa nda ŋiɔn “two sons” Gen 10:25), ŋiin for the i class (palɛi ndii ŋiin “two days” Exod 16:29), miɔn for the an class (polan man miɔn “two rows” 1 Kgs 7:18) and tiɔn for the lan class. Southern Kissi has the same series (ŋìɔ́ɔ́ŋ, ŋìíŋ, mìɔ̀ɔ́ŋ, tìɔ́ɔ́ŋ), whereas “three” varies little there and “four” not at all (Childs 1995, p. 113). The class pronoun attaches there to the number (sálà-láŋ là-tìɔ́ɔ́ŋ “two sacrifices”) (Childs 1995, p. 113); in the Bible, it attaches only to the unit of a compound number (latiɔn).

docs.title: Ordinal numbers
docs.text:
“First” is tasoo Gen 1:1. The other ordinals are formed with -ndɔɔ and agree with the class of the noun:

Ordinal o class i class len class second diinndɔɔ diinndɔɛi third yàándɔɔ fourth hiɔɔlundɔɔ seventh ŋɔmmɛwndɔɔ ŋɔmmɛwndɔlen tenth tɔ́ndɔɔ tɔ́ndɔɛi

Examples: paale ŋɔmmɛwndɔlen “the seventh day” Gen 2:2, paangii tɔ́ndɔɛi “the tenth month” Gen 8:5, paangii diinndɔɛi “the second month” Gen 8:14.

“Second” is diinndɔɔ; tiɔnndɔɔ is very rare Neh 13:6. The stem diin “two” is also found in bidiin “20” and kɛmɛ lediin “200”; Southern Kissi likewise forms “second” on dìíŋ and says “first” with a separate word, tásè (Childs 1995, p. 112, 201).

docs.title: Number of times
docs.text:
The prefix le- forms adverbs of frequency: leyaa “three times”, leŋɔmmɛw “seven times” (Keita 1979, p. 35). See Derivation.

1979 usage

The 1979 arithmetic lessons give the same numbers in the old spelling (Pilè, Tiön, Yaa, Hiöölu, Nhuèènu…, Kèmè lediin, Valan la tiön) (Keita 1979, p. 16-63). The Bible writes tiɔn, ŋuɛɛnu, kɛmɛ, and links the class pronoun to the thousands in the form vàálan tan.

docs.title: Possessives
docs.text:
The possessive is placed after the noun, which takes its stem form: cɛi ndɔɔ “his house”, diola ndɔlan “his name”. It varies according to:

  • the person of the possessor (me, you, him/her, us, you, them);
  • the class and number of the noun possessed;
  • and, in the o class, according to whether what is possessed is a person or a thing.

The construction is the same in Southern Kissi: the noun possessed, followed by its class pronoun (except in the o class), then the possessive carrying the suffix of the noun (Childs 1995, p. 106).

docs.title: Possessed noun of the o class: persons and things
docs.text:
The Bible (BKG) clearly distinguishes two series. With a noun for a person (relative, master, servant), the possessive is short; with a noun for a thing, it carries the class suffix -ndo / -ɔ:

Possessor Person possessed Thing possessed 1st sing. fuɲa nuu “my father” Gen 20:13 kɔl nuu “my heart” Gen 6:13 2nd sing. fuɲa nɔm “your father” Gen 12:1 kɔl nɔmndo “your heart” Josh 14:9 3rd sing. fuɲa ndɔ “his father” Gen 2:24 cɛi ndɔɔ “his house” Gen 39:4 1st plur. fuɲa naa “our father” Gen 19:34 cɛi naa “our house” Song 1:17 2nd plur. fuɲa niaa “your father” Gen 27:6 yoomu niaa “your life” Gen 9:5 3rd plur. fuɲa nda “their father” Gen 9:23 cɛi ndaa “their house” Neh 3:23

The short forms nɔm, ndɔ, nda are those of the object pronouns. A few nouns are used with both series depending on the meaning: po ndɔ “his son” (172 times) but po ndɔɔ (67 times).

Rule

For a relative or a person: kala ndɔ “his mother” Gen 2:24, laa nɔm “your wife” Gen 3:17. For a thing: fonda ndɔɔ “his place” Gen 36:33, kɔl nɔmndo “your heart”.

docs.title: General table (Bible)
docs.text:
Possessor o (thing) plural persons i plur. -on an len lan 1st sing. nuu nia nii nian nilen nilan 2nd sing. nɔmndo nɔmnda nɔmnde nɔmndon nɔmndan nɔmnden nɔmndan 3rd sing. ndɔɔ ndɔa ndɔɛi ndɔn ndɔan ndɔlen ndɔlan 1st plur. naa naa naan naalen naalan 2nd plur. niaa niaa niɛi niaan niaalen niaalan 3rd plur. ndaa ndaa ndɛi ndan ndan ndalen ndalan

Examples:

  • i: sɔɛi nii “my word” Gen 22:18, sɔɛi ndɛi “their language” Gen 11:7;
  • -on: vanayan nɔmndon “your kindred” Gen 12:1;
  • an: yoomuma nian “my strength” Gen 31:6, kooma ndɔan “its blood” Exod 12:7;
  • len: lɛŋnde nilen “my land” Gen 20:15, lɛŋnde naalen “our land” Gen 26:16;
  • lan: silala nilan “my laws” Gen 26:5, diola ndalan “their names” Gen 10:32;
  • plural persons: vanaa nia bɛndua “my lords” Gen 18:3, poaa ndɔa “his sons” Gen 7:7, cuavaa naa “our children” Gen 31:16.

In Southern Kissi too, the 1st person singular possessive has two forms, nù and nì, like nuu and ni- (nii, nilen) in the Bible; the possessives there have a low tone, whereas the object pronouns have a high tone (Childs 1995, p. 106).

1st sing. with plural persons, and 2nd plur.

The Bible distinguishes nia “my” (with plural persons) and niaa “your” (plural possessor): vanaa nia “my lords”, fuɲaa niaa “your fathers”. The 1979 spelling writes both as niaa (Keita 1979, p. 61).

docs.title: Possessive pronouns
docs.text: To say “mine, yours…”, the possessive is preceded by the class pronoun (Keita 1979, p. 60-62): o nuu “mine” (o class), i nii (i class), le nilen (len class), la nilan (lan class), ma nian (an class).

docs.title: Other ways of expressing possession
docs.text:
Two other constructions are found (Keita 1979, p. 62-63):

  1. with the verb nɔw “have” and the particle ni: Tamba nɔ cɛiyo hoo ni “Tamba has this house”;
  2. with the class referent and ni: Naw Fatee vo ni “It is Fatee’s cow”.

In the Bible, a named possessor is placed after the noun possessed, followed by the class referent: lɛŋnde Esipte len “the land of Egypt” Gen 13:10, nakɔ Mɛlɛka-o “the garden of the Lord” Gen 13:10.

1979 usage

The 1979 spelling writes the 2nd person num- (nummdo, nummde) (Keita 1979, p. 61); the Bible writes nɔm-: nɔmndo, nɔmnde. The 1979 forms of the 1st and 2nd plur. for the len and lan classes (nialen, nialan) are niaalen, niaalan in the Bible.

docs.title: Compound nouns
docs.text: Kisiei forms many new nouns by combining two or more words. Eight types are distinguished (Keita 1979, p. 31-33); the Bible (BKG) makes considerable use of them for new notions.

docs.title: Types of compounds
docs.text:
Type 1979 example (respelled) Example (Bible) Meaning noun + noun mɔmɔtɔmndo “fruit that monkeys love” (rice + monkey) fuɲa-mamaa ancestor (father + grandparent) noun + verb peekolaa “well” (water + drink) ɲɛdiaa food (thing + eat) noun + adjective naasiaŋaa “leprosy” (illness + red) kɔlvesɛiyo violence, wickedness (heart + dry, hard) noun + verb + negation tɔmcilon “variety of maize” (monkey + see + not) noun + referent + noun kelamaɲumndan “night-time stroll” noun + linking word + noun cɔwlabaa “fight” (war + of + hand)

The noun + referent + noun type corresponds to the general pattern described for Southern Kissi, where the second noun is preceded by its own class pronoun (Childs 1995, p. 209-210): in kelamaɲumndan, ma is the class pronoun of ɲumndan “night”. Southern Kissi also forms compounds from a verb or from an adjective derived from a verb (Childs 1995, p. 211).

docs.title: Compounds in the Bible
docs.text:
The Bible creates many compounds for religious, legal or technical realities; Southern Kissi likewise names new objects with compounds (Childs 1995, p. 210-211). They are almost always written with hyphens between their parts:

Compound Parts Meaning vana-solia-lasálàá person + who offers + sacrifice priest Gen 41:45 fonda-loamaa-lasálàá place + burn + sacrifice altar Gen 8:20 vana-tɛɛngaa-diom person + between + word prophet Gen 20:7 vanaa-mangalaa-isɔɔa people + … peoples, nations Gen 12:2 cɛi-kola house + cloth tent Gen 9:21 fuɲa-mamaa father + grandparent ancestor Gen 17:4

Old and very common compounds are written as a single word:

Compound Parts Meaning vanapɔnɔɔ person + male man vanalanɔɔ person + female woman vanacieo person + village human being ɲɛdiaa thing + eat food halataalaa (God, sky) + … heaven, sky

Spelling rule

  • A fixed, common compound is written as a single word (vanapɔnɔɔ).
  • A descriptive compound, each part of which keeps its meaning, is written with hyphens (vana-solia-lasálàá).
  • In the singular, the first element is in the stem form (fuɲa-, not fuɲaa-).
  • In the plural, it is the first element that takes the plural marking: vanaa-solia-lasálàá “the priests” Gen 47:22, fuɲaa-mamaa “ancestors” Gen 10:32; in some compounds, each element takes it: cɛila-kolala-toandaalan “tents” Gen 13:5.

In Southern Kissi too, it is the first noun, the head of the compound, that marks number through its class pronoun, and its suffix moves to the end of the compound (Childs 1995, p. 209-210).

docs.title: Compound proper names
docs.text: There are also compound first names made up of the birth-order name and an event linked to the birth (Keita 1979, p. 32): Tamba lɔɔ “Tamba born on market day”, Saa muuloo “Saa born during the tax period”.

docs.title: Derivation
docs.text: Derivation forms new nouns by adding a suffix or a prefix to a stem. A distinction is made between pure derivatives (suffixes) and lexical derivatives (former nouns that have become prefixes) (Keita 1979, p. 34-40). Unless otherwise stated, the examples below are taken from the Bible (BKG).

docs.title: -nɔɔ: person who does, person of
docs.text:
The suffix -nɔɔ (plural -nda or -a) forms nouns for people:

  • origin, people: Esiptenɔɔ “Egyptian” Gen 16:1, Israɛlnɔɔ “Israelite”, Filistinɔɔ “Philistine”;
  • occupation, function: kpalilnɔɔ “guard, watchman” 2 Sam 18:24, kiilanɔɔ “messenger” Gen 50:16, mandenɔɔ “marabout, diviner”;
  • quality: kuubanɔɔ “hero”, langbanɔɔ “grown man”.

Southern Kissi has the same agent suffix, -nɔ̀ɔ́, with a plural in -a (Childs 1995, p. 198-199).

The same suffix also forms family names (Kambadunɔɔ) and names for speakers of a language (Kisinɔɔ “a Kisi person”) (Keita 1979, p. 35).

docs.title: -yɛi: quality, state
docs.text:
The suffix -yɛi forms abstract nouns:

Base Derivative Meaning vana “person” vanayɛi kinship cuaambɔɔ “child” cuaambɔyɛi childhood felengoo “young” felengiyɛi youth Gen 8:21 vanakɛndɛ “good person” vanakɛndɛyɛi goodness, righteousness 1 Sam 24:19 hɔ́ɔ́ “free” hɔ́ɔ́yɛi freedom Exod 21:2

docs.title: -ndɔɔ: rank (ordinals)
docs.text: Added to a number, -ndɔɔ forms the ordinal: ŋɔmmɛwndɔɔ “seventh”, like -ndɔ̀ɔ́ in Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 200-201). See Numbers.

docs.title: -len: diminutive
docs.text: The suffix -len (len class) can form diminutives (Keita 1979, p. 23, 35): pɔmbɔlen “very small”, and, from animal names, nouns for human faults or qualities (tunnden “filth”, from tunndo “dog”). In Southern Kissi too, the le class is used to form diminutives and most abstract nouns (Childs 1995, p. 166, 203).

docs.title: i-…-ei: state
docs.text: A discontinuous form i-…-ei forms nouns of state (Keita 1979, p. 37): ilafilafiei “always being in a hurry”. This type is rare in the Bible; it remains to be confirmed with speakers.

docs.title: le-: number of times
docs.text: Prefixed to a number, le- expresses repetition (Keita 1979, p. 35): leyaa “three times”, leŋɔmmɛw “seven times”.

docs.title: Prefixes derived from nouns
docs.text:
Several nouns are used as the first element of many derivatives; they then lose their suffix:

Prefix Source noun Derivatives (Bible) ɲɛ- “thing” ɲɛ ɲɛdiaa “food”, ɲɛkɛndɛi “good thing, happiness”, ɲɛ-sɔlaa “wealth”, ɲɛ-tengaa “light” kɔl- “heart” kɔllo kɔlɲuloo “comfort, rest” Gen 5:29, kɔlvesɛiyo “violence” Gen 6:13, kɔltuwvo “anger” Exod 11:8, kɔlkɛndɔɔ “joy” vana- “person” vana vanacieo “human being”, vanayɛi “kinship”, vana-solia-lasálàá “priest” dɛnɛ “deed, thing” dɛnɛ dɛnɛ kɛndɔɔ “good”, dɛnɛ vɔɔndo “evil” Gen 2:9

vana- corresponds to the agent prefix wànà- of Southern Kissi, which is likewise derived from the word “person” (Childs 1995, p. 199-200). The word “thing” there likewise enters into so many compounds that it becomes almost a prefix (Childs 1995, p. 216).

1979 usage

In 1979 one also finds ba- “hand” (bamɛllo “left hand”) and dɛnɛ- written attached (dɛnɛkɛndɔɔ) (Keita 1979, p. 38-39). The Bible writes dɛnɛ as a separate word: dɛnɛ kɛndɔɔ.

docs.title: Reduplication
docs.text: Reduplicating a word or a stem forms a derivative expressing intensity, distribution or repetition; it is written with a hyphen: taw-taw “really a lot”, ɲɛ-ɲɛ “anything at all”, vana-vana “anyone at all”, bɛndu-bɛnduan “very great”.

docs.title: The noun
docs.text:
The Kisiei noun consists of a stem and a class suffix. The class determines the plural of the noun and the form of all the words that agree with it.

  • Noun classes: the suffixes, the full form and the stem form;
  • Plural: how to go from singular to plural;
  • Compound nouns: noun + noun, noun + verb, compounds in the Bible;
  • Derivation: suffixes -nɔɔ, -yɛi, -ndɔɔ, prefixes derived from nouns, reduplication.

The agreement of other words with the noun is described on the Agreement page.

docs.title: The principle
docs.text:
Every Kisiei noun consists of a stem, which carries the meaning, and a class suffix (also called morpheme or nominal modality (Keita 1979, p. 20-22)), which indicates the class of the noun and its number:

Noun Stem Suffix Meaning yɔmndo yɔm -ndo tree cɛiyo cɛi -yo house diolan diola -n (lan class) name mɛnndan mɛn- -ndan water nawvo naw -vo cow

The suffix is not just a word ending: it comes back on the words that accompany the noun (determiners, pronouns, relatives). This is the agreement system described on the Agreement page.

docs.title: Full form and stem form
docs.text:
The noun has two forms:

  • the full form (stem + suffix): when the noun stands alone, or at the end of a phrase;
  • the stem form (stem alone): when the noun is followed by a word that determines it — adjective, demonstrative, possessive, number, noun complement. The suffix then moves onto that word.
Full form Stem form + determiner cɛiyo “the house” cɛi kon “that house” yɔmndo “the tree” yɔm kon “that tree” diolan “the name” diola ndɔlan “his name” kalaa “the mother” kala ndɔ “his mother” pɔmbɔɔ “the younger sibling” pɔmbɔ ndɔ “his younger brother”

The stem form is also called the indefinite form, and the full form the definite form (Keita 1979, p. 20); the full form indeed plays the role of the French definite article, which Kisiei does not have.

Rule

The suffix is never written twice: cɛiyo kon is wrong; write cɛi kon.

docs.title: lan, len and an classes: stem + class pronoun
docs.text:
In the o class, the stem form is the bare stem (cɛi kon). In the lan, len and an classes, the Bible (BKG) writes before the determiner the stem followed by the class pronoun without its final nasal: -la, -le, -ma. After a nasal, -le becomes -nde; after l, -lle. The 1979 manual mentions this only for the an class (Keita 1979, p. 122); the same construction is described in Southern Kissi (“noun + class pronoun + adjective”) (Childs 1995, p. 150).

Full form Stem form Example (Bible) diolan “name” diola diola ndalan “their names” Gen 10:32 kobilan “cities” kobila kobila lan “these cities” Gen 19:25 lɛŋnden “land” lɛŋnde lɛŋnde Havila len “the land of Havilah” Gen 2:11 bollen “head” bolle bolle ndɔlen “its top” Gen 11:4 nilen “ear” nile nile tiilannde “the lobe of the ear” Exod 29:20 mɛnndan “water” mɛmma mɛmma co lebɛngu-an “the waters that are below” Gen 1:7 koovan “blood” kooma kooma pɔmbɔ nɔmndan “your brother’s blood” Gen 4:10 cuɛiyan “oil” cuɛima

Plurals in -lan follow the same rule: their stem form ends in -la (-nda after a nasal), as in the Bible: tɔŋnda nilan “my commandments” Gen 26:5, yungula “the families” Gen 10:32, vɔsila bɔɔ-bɔɔ “many years” Gen 24:1.

Rule

Before a determiner, write as a single word: stem + la (lan class), stem + le / nde / lle (len class), stem + ma (an class): diola ndɔlan, lɛŋnde len, mɛmma man.

flowchart TD
    N["A noun"] --> Q{"Is it followed by a word that determines it?<br>(adjective, demonstrative, possessive,<br>number, noun complement)"}
    Q -- no --> F["Full form<br><i>cɛiyo</i>, <i>diolan</i>, <i>lɛŋnden</i>"]
    Q -- yes --> C{"Class of the noun?"}
    C -- "o" --> R1["Bare stem<br><i>cɛi kon</i>"]
    C -- "lan" --> R2["Stem + <i>-la</i><br><i>diola ndɔlan</i>"]
    C -- "len" --> R3["Stem + <i>-le / -nde / -lle</i><br><i>lɛŋnde len</i>"]
    C -- "an" --> R4["Stem + <i>-ma</i><br><i>mɛmma man</i>"]
Full form or stem form? Before a determiner, the lan, len and an classes add the class pronoun to the stem.

docs.title: The classes
docs.text:
Eight suffixes are distinguished (Keita 1979, p. 22-25), grouped here into classes according to their plural and their referents. The suffixes have variants that depend on the end of the stem (after a nasal, -nd- is found; after l, -l- or -t-; after w, -v-; after i, -y-). The same variants are described for Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 151-156).

Class Singular suffixes Typical content Examples (Bible) o / a / ɔ -o, -ndo, -vo, -lo, -yo; -a; -ɔ living beings (people, animals) and many objects yɔmndo “tree”, nawvo “cow”, kalaa “mother”, pɔmbɔɔ “younger sibling”, miallo “stranger” i -i, -ei, -ɛi certain solid objects, names of languages pelei “foot”, mɔɛi “knife”, kelɛi “bracelet”, sɔɛi “word” e -e, -ye, -nde, -ve, -le grains, countable objects, collections ciŋnde “tooth”, yɛiye “seed” an -an, -yan, -van, -ndan liquids, masses mɛnndan “water”, koovan “blood”, cuɛiyan “oil” lan -lan, -tan, -ndan abstract nouns; and the plural of many nouns diolan “name”, yolan “dance” len -len, -ten, -nden fruits, certain body parts, soft objects; diminutives nilen “ear”, bollen “head”, lɛŋnden “land”

The i and e series form a single class in Southern Kissi: there the ending -e becomes -ei or -ɛi after a stem ending in a vowel (Childs 1995, p. 148, 153). The Bible points the same way: nouns of both series are taken up by the same pronoun i, have the same referent -e (see Agreement) and the same plural in -on.

The main meanings are also found in Southern Kissi: grains and names of languages in the i class, diminutives in the le (len) class, liquids in the ma (an) class (Childs 1995, p. 165-169). Abstract nouns, on the other hand, belong there mostly to the le class (Childs 1995, p. 169).

The plural is covered on the Plural page.

Comparison: Southern Kissi

For Southern Kissi, the classes are named after their pronoun (Childs 1995, p. 148-149): o, a, i, ŋ, le, la, ma. The most frequent singular/plural pairs are o/la (things), o/a (people, animals) and i/ŋ; next come le/i, le/la, le/ma and o/i. The plural in -on of the 1979 description (pelon, sɔɔn) corresponds to the ŋ class of that analysis. The same system is found in Kisiei of Guinea, with different forms in the details.

docs.title: What the Bible shows
docs.text:
The Bible confirms the broad outlines of the system described in 1979: full form and stem form, class suffixes and repetition of the class on determiners. It adds two clarifications:

  1. Suffixes in -nd- keep the final nasal of the stem, whether it is n or ŋ: mɛnndan (stem mɛn-), but lɛŋnden (stem lɛŋ). See Consonants.
  2. When a noun phrase ends with a relative clause or a complement, the class of the noun is taken up again at the end of the phrase by a referent attached with a hyphen (kɔngɔ vesɛi fula-o). See Agreement.

docs.title: Masculine and feminine
docs.text: Kisiei has no grammatical gender. To specify the sex of a being, piaando “male” or laando “female” is added to the stem form (Keita 1979, p. 28): so piaando “stallion”, so laando “mare”. The same device is described in Southern Kissi for animals (Childs 1995, p. 216-217). The Bible uses these words in the plural for children: a piaandua a à laandua “sons and daughters” Gen 5:4.

docs.title: Plural
docs.text:
The plural is formed by replacing the singular suffix with a plural suffix. Which suffix? That depends on the class of the noun and, for the o / a / ɔ class, on what the noun refers to (Keita 1979, p. 26-29). All the pairs below are attested in the Bible (BKG).

flowchart TD
    N["Singular noun"] --> C{"Class?"}
    C -- "o / a / ɔ" --> P{"Person<br>or animal?"}
    P -- yes --> A["<i>-a</i> (<i>-nda, -la, -va</i>)<br><i>nawvo</i> → <i>nawva</i>"]
    P -- no --> L["<i>-lan</i> (<i>-tan, -ndan</i>)<br><i>kobio</i> → <i>kobilan</i>"]
    C -- "i" --> I{"Ending?"}
    I -- "-ei" --> I1["<i>-on</i><br><i>pelei</i> → <i>pelon</i>"]
    I -- "-ɛi" --> I2["<i>-ɔn</i><br><i>sɔɛi</i> → <i>sɔɔn</i>"]
    C -- "e" --> E["<i>-on</i><br><i>yɛiye</i> → <i>yɛiyon</i>"]
    C -- "len" --> LE["<i>-an, -lan, -tan</i><br><i>nilen</i> → <i>nilan</i>"]
Choosing the plural suffix. Exceptions and nouns without a plural are covered below.

docs.title: People and animals: -a
docs.text:
Nouns for people and animals in -o, -ɔ or -a form their plural in -a (-nda after a nasal, -la after l, -va after w). In Southern Kissi too, the o / a pair covers practically all animate beings (Childs 1995, p. 163-164):

Singular Plural Meaning nawvo nawva cow(s) yowvo yowva bird(s) kɛwvo kɛwva snake(s) cuinndo cuinnda goat(s) miallo mialla stranger(s) vanndo vannda person(s), people pɔmbɔɔ pɔmbɔa younger sibling(s) poo poaa son(s) lanɔɔ laandua woman/women, wife/wives cuaa cuavaa child(ren); in the singular, often “(young) woman” (Gen 3:13)

docs.title: Things in -o, -a, -ɔ: -lan
docs.text:
Nouns for things in -o, -ɔ or -a form their plural in -lan (-tan after l, -ndan after a nasal). This is the most frequent pair in Southern Kissi (o / la), where it also takes in loanwords (Childs 1995, p. 149, 163):

Singular Plural Meaning kobio kobilan town(s) domaa domalan shirt(s), garment(s) naa naalan illness(es) paa paalan bone(s)

docs.title: i class: -on, -ɔn, -an
docs.text:
Nouns in -ei form their plural in -on; those in -ɛi, in -ɔn (Keita 1979, p. 27-28). This is the i / ŋ pair of Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 164):

Singular Plural Meaning pelei pelon foot/feet suei suon finger(s) mɔɛi mɔɔn knife/knives sɔɛi sɔɔn word(s) kelɛi kelan bracelet(s) — exception in -an

docs.title: e class: -on
docs.text: Singular Plural Meaning yɛiye yɛiyon seed(s) kulle kullon grain(s)

docs.title: len class: -an, -lan, -tan
docs.text: Singular Plural Meaning nilen nilan ear(s) bollen bóltan head(s) pelten (Keita 1979, p. 28) peltan egg(s)

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
The following exceptions appear in the 1979 description (Keita 1979, p. 27):

  • -o → -e: kollo / kolle “kola nut”, hollo / holle “mushroom”.
  • -o → -on: cieo / cieon “village(s)”, kilio / kilion.
  • Invariable: saa “sheep”, yangaa “shrimp(s)”, ɲinaa “spirit(s), demon(s)”.

The first two types correspond to rarer pairs also described for Southern Kissi, o / i and o / ŋ; the word for “town, village” appears there precisely in the o / ŋ pair (Childs 1995, p. 149, 167).

docs.title: Nouns without a plural
docs.text:
• Masses and liquids are used only in the singular: hɛlle “salt”, mɛnndan “water”.
  • Neither are abstract nouns: diolan “name”, hangullo “heat”, ɲumndan “darkness”.
  • Some collectives exist only in the plural: diallon “the body”.

Southern Kissi also classes “name” and “darkness” among nouns without a plural (Childs 1995, p. 169-170).

docs.title: Plural and agreement
docs.text:
The plural also changes the words that agree with the noun. People in the plural are taken up by nda “them”, things in -lan by lan, and so on: poaa ndɔa “his sons”, diola ndɔlan “his name”. See Agreement.

Note

For a noun not found in the Bible, follow these rules, but the plural form must be confirmed by a speaker: several nouns have irregular plurals (about a dozen are listed in the 1979 description (Keita 1979, p. 26-29)).

docs.title: Pronouns
docs.text:
• Personal pronouns: subject pronouns, independent pronouns, class pronouns, narrative forms (mí, mó, má);
  • Relative clauses: the relative clause framed by the class of the noun, and the subjects of relative clauses.

docs.title: Personal pronouns
docs.text: Kisiei has two main series of personal pronouns: the subject pronouns, which are short and placed before the verb, and the independent pronouns, which serve as objects, as emphasized subjects and as possessives for persons (Keita 1979, p. 85-87).

docs.title: Table
docs.text:
Person Subject Independent / object Emphatic Example (Bible) 1st sing. i ya ya pila “myself” I tuisinin nɔm “I will put on you” Gen 3:16 2nd sing. a nɔm nɔm pila le nɔm pila “for yourself” Gen 14:21 3rd sing. o ndu ndu pila mó yaa nda “he brought them” Gen 2:19 1st plur. n naa naa pila N kɔ delnun ndu coo “let us go and throw ourselves on him” Gen 37:20 2nd plur. la niaa niaa pila Niaa pila bɛɛ la sina “you yourselves know” Gen 31:6 3rd plur. a nda nda pila A ve sina “they did not know” Gen 42:23

Spelling rules

  • Pronouns are written separately from the verb: I tuei, N kɔɛ.
  • The emphatic word pila “self” is written separately: ya pila, nda pila (1979: yapila (Keita 1979, p. 85)).
  • The 2nd person singular is written nɔm (1979: num, corrected by hand to nöm (Keita 1979, p. 85)).

In relative clauses and questions, subjects take another series: ya, n “you (sing.)”, o, naa n, niaa, ndáà; see Relative clauses.

docs.title: 3rd-person pronouns by class
docs.text:
When the pronoun replaces a thing, it takes the form of the noun’s class (see Agreement):

Class Subject Object o (sing.) o ndu plural persons a nda i i ndi plur. in -on n mun an ma man len le len lan la lan

Examples: Tɛyii tasei diolan Pison, ndi balu lɛŋnde Havila len ni “The first river is called Pishon; it is the one (ndi) that flows around the land of Havilah” Gen 2:11; kobilan la va belaŋɔmpum “the cities (la) were sixty” Deut 3:4.

Note: a is both “you (sing.)” and “they”; la is both “you (plur.)” and the pronoun of the lan class; n is “we” and the pronoun of plurals in -on. The context removes the ambiguity.

docs.title: Pronouns and narrative markers
docs.text:
In narrative, the subject pronoun combines with the marker mi (“and then”):

Form Analysis Example mí + noun “and (the noun)…” Mí Hala dimi aa “And God said” Gen 1:3 mó mi + o “and he/she” mó yaa nda “and he brought them” Gen 2:19 má mi + a “and they” má kuumbuu “and they covered” Gen 9:23 mí n, mí la, mí ya i mi + another pronoun mí n komal Esau “and we met Esau” Gen 32:7

In Southern Kissi, the same fusion gives mi, ma, mbo, miŋ, mila, ma (Childs 1995, p. 75, 107). The low-tone forms mò, mà, mì mark the subjunctive (“so that he…”); see Tense, aspect, mood and Tones.

The independent pronoun also combines with the past vowel oo / aa (1979: ndu oo, ya oo (Keita 1979, p. 87)). The Bible (BKG) writes it as a single word, with tones: ndóò “he, she (had)”, ndáà “they (had)”, yáà “I (had)”: yɔmndo ndu pilɛ bɛɛ ndóò vil-lɔ o lɛŋnden coo le “no tree had yet grown on the earth” Gen 2:5.

docs.title: The independent pronoun as subject
docs.text:
The independent pronoun can replace the subject pronoun to emphasize the person (Keita 1979, p. 86): Ndu yɔngu ya ni “It is he who gave it to me”. In the Bible: Nda yɔŋnun kuubaa “It was they who became heroes” Gen 6:4. The independent pronoun is often followed by the subject pronoun: Niaa pila bɛɛ la sina “you yourselves know” Gen 31:6. Southern Kissi uses the same two constructions, for emphasis or contrast (Childs 1995, p. 105-106).

Comparison

In Southern Kissi, the subject pronouns are í, à, ò, ŋ̀, là, à and the object pronouns yá, nùm, ndú, náá, ɲá, ndá (Childs 1995, p. 104-105): the subjects have a low tone (except í “I”), the objects a high tone. The differences from the Bible lie mainly in the spelling (ŋ̀ for n “we”) and in the 2nd person plural (ɲá for niaa). The Wikipedia article on Northern Kissi gives similar forms; it writes y for “I” before a vowel and aa for “they”, where the Bible writes i and a.

docs.title: Relative clauses
docs.text: Kisiei has no separate relative pronoun like English who, which, that (French qui, que). The relative clause is framed by the class of the noun: the noun loses its suffix, the relative clause follows, and the class suffix comes back at the end of the relative clause, attached by a hyphen to the last word. The rules on this page are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG); the same structure is described for Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 285-288).

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
noun (stem form) + [clause] + -class suffix

Example (Bible) Analysis Meaning kɔngɔ vesɛi fula-o kɔngɔ vesɛi [fula]-o the dry land that appeared Gen 1:10 mɛmma co lebɛngu-an mɛm-ma [co lebɛngu]-an the waters that are below Gen 1:7 visia pɔmbɔa kela lɛŋ-nda visia pɔmbɔa [kela lɛŋ]-nda the small creatures that move on the ground Gen 1:24 sɔɛi Mɛlɛka dimul ndu-e sɔɛi [Mɛlɛka dimul ndu]-e the word that the Lord had spoken to him Gen 15:6 lɔma ya sɔl-lan lɔma [ya sɔl]-lan the dream that I had Gen 37:6 lɛŋnde ya co nɔm cɔm-nden lɛŋnde [ya co nɔm cɔm]-nden the land that I will show you Gen 12:1 ɲɛm vanaa kan ndáà manda le dioo-on ɲɛm [vanaa kan ndáà manda le dioo]-on the provisions that those people had kept to eat Gen 14:11 
flowchart LR
    N["Noun, stem form<br><i>lɛŋnde</i><br>“the land”"] --> R["Clause<br><i>ya co nɔm cɔm</i><br>“I will show you”"]
    R --> T["Class suffix<br><i>-nden</i>"]
    T -. "same class: <i>len</i>" .-> N
    classDef cls stroke:#d07a2a,stroke-width:3px
    class N,T cls
The relative clause is framed by the class of the noun: lɛŋnde ya co nɔm cɔm-nden “the land that I will show you” (Gen 12:1).

In the an, len and lan classes, the noun keeps its class pronoun before the relative clause (mɛmma = mɛm- + ma, lɛŋnde, kobila), as before an adjective; in the o class, the stem is bare (kɔngɔ). See Noun classes.

Often a demonstrative hoo “this” or kon “that” is placed at the end of the relative clause, just before the suffix: Kpema ya yii hoo-o “the covenant that I establish” Gen 17:7, fonda n sim kon-ndo “the place where you are standing” Gen 13:14, dɛnɛ n tosa hoo-o “the thing that you have done” Gen 3:14. Southern Kissi also uses a demonstrative inside the relative clause, especially when the relativized noun is placed at the start of the sentence as the topic (Childs 1995, p. 288-289).

docs.title: The final suffix
docs.text:
The suffix that closes the relative clause is that of the noun’s class; it changes form according to the last sound of the word to which it attaches, exactly like noun suffixes (Childs 1995, p. 151-153):

Class after a vowel after a nasal after l after i o (sing.) -o: fula-o -ndo: nin-ndo -lo: hɔl-lo -yo: paangei-yo plural persons -a: coocoo-a -nda: lɛŋ-nda -la -ya: ikɛi-ya i -e: ndu-e -nde: can-nde -le: del-le -ye an -an: lebɛngu-an -ndan: nin-ndan -tan -yan len -len -nden: cɔm-nden -ten: Israɛl-ten lan -lan -ndan -lan: sɔl-lan plur. in -on -on: dioo-on -ndon: mún-ndon -lon -yon: landei-yon

After w, -o, -a and -on become -vo, -va, -von (cɔw-von Gen 1:31).

docs.title: The subject of the relative clause
docs.text:
In the relative clause, the subject pronouns are not those of the simple sentence (i, a, o…): they form a series of their own, the same as in questions.

Person Simple sentence Relative clause, question Example (Bible) 1st sing. i ya lɔma ya sɔl-lan “the dream that I had” Gen 37:6 2nd sing. a n dɛnɛ n tosa hoo-o “the thing that you have done” Gen 3:14; fonda n yeema-o “the place that you want” Gen 13:9 3rd sing. o o ɲɛm o cɔw-von “the things that he had made” Gen 1:31 1st plur. n naa n lɔma naa n sɔl man-ndan “the dreams that we had” Gen 41:12 2nd plur. la niaa lɔma niaa sɔl-lan “the dream that you had” Gen 40:8 3rd plur. a ndáà ɲɛm ndáà yoo ndu-on “the things that they brought him” Gen 43:26

Note: n means “you (sing.)” in a relative clause or a question, but “we” in the simple sentence.

When the noun itself is the subject of the relative clause, the verb follows directly: kɔngɔ vesɛi fula-o.

docs.title: Relative clauses of place or time
docs.text:
Nouns of place and time are relativized in the same way:

  • fonda ni ya va baalaa-o “the place where I used to work” Gen 41:13;
  • kobila va o dɛɛla kon nin-ndan “the cities that were in that plain” Gen 13:12.

Spelling rules

  • The class suffix that closes the relative clause is attached to the last word of the relative clause with a hyphen: fula-o, sɔl-lan, cɔm-nden.
  • The hyphen is used even if the last word is a postposition (coo-o, nin-ndan) or a proper noun (Israɛl-ten).
  • Do not write the suffix as a separate word.

1979 usage

The 1979 description presents these suffixes as separate relative pronouns, placed after the verb: vo, ve, van, len, lan, plural va, von (Keita 1979, p. 88-89) (Domaa n pendu vo sèsa “the shirt that you bought is beautiful”). The Bible attaches them to the last word of the relative clause with a hyphen; this usage is authoritative. See Word division.

docs.title: The complex sentence
docs.text: The rules on this page are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG). The conjunctions themselves are presented on the Prepositions, postpositions and conjunctions page.

docs.title: Narrative sequence: mí, mó, má
docs.text:
Narrative links clauses together with mí + pronoun (high tone): Mí Hala dimi aa … Mí ɲɔɔ tosan lende “And God said… And it was so” Gen 1:6-7. Each new action is a clause introduced by mí, mó or má; see Tense, aspect, mood.

flowchart LR
    A["A clause<br><i>Mí Hala dimi aa …</i>"] -- "<i>mí</i> / <i>mó</i> / <i>má</i>: high tone" --> B["Next action, completed<br>“and (then) …”<br><i>Mí ɲɔɔ tosan lende</i>"]
    A2["A clause<br><i>N cɔwnun vanacieo a velan naa</i>"] -- "<i>mì</i> / <i>mò</i> / <i>mà</i>: low tone" --> C["Intended action<br>“so that, and may …”<br><i>mò vel naa</i>"]
Linking (high tone) or aiming at a purpose (low tone): the tone of mi + pronoun makes the difference (Gen 1:6-7; Gen 1:26).

docs.title: Purpose and consequence
docs.text: Construction Meaning Example mì / mò / mà + verb so that, and may N cɔwnun vanacieo a velan naa, mò vel naa “Let us make man in our image, so that he resembles us” Gen 1:26 haliko mi … in order that haliko mi la va baloo dɔwnɔnndo “so that it may be your food” Gen 1:29 le + long form in order to (do) le dioo “to eat” Gen 3:11

docs.title: Cause
docs.text: kani “for, because” and le tùú “because” introduce the cause: kani o falun vanapɔnɔɔ nin “for she was taken out of man” Gen 2:23; Le tùú n cɛl sɔɛi laa nɔm-nde “because you listened to the voice of your wife” Gen 3:17. lelan and le hee “that is why” introduce the consequence Gen 2:24.

docs.title: Condition: te … pɛ
docs.text:
The condition opens with te and closes with pɛ, placed just after the verb of the condition; the consequence follows:

  • te o de pɛ kɔmnde yɔm kon, o co vannɔn yoomu le fɛɛn a fɛɛn “if he eats of the fruit of this tree, he will live for ever” Gen 3:22;
  • unreal condition with the lengthened pronoun: te yáà de pɛ visin “if I had eaten meat” Lev 10:19.

A negative condition keeps pɛ and places the negation at the end of the condition: Kɛ taa liila ya le, i kuenin te “but if you do not come with me, I will not go” Judg 4:8 (taa = te + a “if you”).

flowchart TB
    subgraph COND["Condition"]
        direction LR

    end
    COND --> C["Consequence<br><i>o co vannɔn yoomu le fɛɛn a fɛɛn</i>"]
