    class T,P mark
The condition opened by te and closed by pɛ right after the verb, then the consequence (Gen 3:22).

docs.title: Time
docs.text: Mɛɛ “when” and Tuma “at the time when” open a time clause, often closed by a class referent: Tuma Mɛlɛka Hala cɔw halataalaa a lɛŋnden-ndo “When the Lord God made the heavens and the earth” Gen 2:4; Mɛɛ Hala cii baala kon tosa kpow, mó mal vallo “When God had finished his work, he rested” Gen 2:2.

docs.title: Complement clauses
docs.text: After verbs of saying, seeing, knowing and wanting, the complement clause is introduced by maa: mó ca maa n naŋ taw “he saw that it was very good” Gen 1:31; I sina nihau válán maa a nɔ siòòŋii Hala-e “now I know that you fear God” Gen 22:12.

docs.title: Relative clauses
docs.text:
See Relative clauses.

Spelling rules

  • A comma separates the condition or the time clause from the main clause: te o de pɛ kɔmnde yɔm kon, …
  • taa (“if you”) is written as one word, as in the Bible.

docs.title: The sentence
docs.text:
• Word order: subject – verb – object, resumptive pronoun, focus;
  • The simple sentence: verbal sentence, identification, possession, serial verbs, reported speech;
  • The complex sentence: narrative, purpose, cause, condition, time, complement clauses.

docs.title: The simple sentence
docs.text: The rules on this page are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG).

docs.title: Verbal sentence
docs.text: The verbal sentence consists of a subject (noun or pronoun), a verb and its objects and complements: Mí Kain del Abɛl pɔmbɔ ndɔ coo Gen 4:8. Tense and aspect are carried by the verb, the auxiliary and the pronoun (see Tense, aspect, mood).

docs.title: Sentences of identification and existence
docs.text: Construction Meaning Example (Bible) X co Y ni X is Y (identity) Hoo co masa Yuifia ni “This is the king of the Jews” Luke 23:38 X co + place X is (located) at… Mɛlɛka co o fondaa ho “the Lord is in this place” Gen 28:16 X va + place, state X was… Lɛŋnden le va tulumasaa “the earth was formless” Gen 1:2 X ni it is X Paale taselen le yɔŋnun nden ni “that was the first day” Gen 1:5 X co … le X is not… O co dɛnɛ vana bɛnda le tosa le Gen 20:9

docs.title: Possession: “to have”
docs.text: “To have” is expressed with the verb nɔ: tɔ́ɔ́ pila ndáà nɔ ni “they had strength” Gen 6:4; Noe ndóò nɔ vɔsilan kɛmɛ leŋɔmpum “Noah was six hundred years old” Gen 7:6.

docs.title: Serial verbs
docs.text:
Two verbs can follow each other to describe a single complex action:

  • hun a “come with” = bring: mí Kain hun a ɲɛm “Cain brought some produce” Gen 4:3;
  • kɔ + verb “go and do”: Mí Abram kɔ hun a cɔlua kan “Abram went and fetched these animals” Gen 15:10; N kɔ delnun ndu coo “let us go and fall upon him” Gen 37:20.

docs.title: Reported speech
docs.text: Speech is introduced by a verb of saying followed by aa and a colon: Mí Hala dimi aa: “And God said:” Gen 1:3; mó dimul ndu aa: “he said to him:” Gen 3:17. See Punctuation.

docs.title: Questions and commands
docs.text: Questions are described on the Interrogatives page, commands on the Tense, aspect, mood page, and negation on the Negation page.

docs.title: Word order
docs.text: The rules on this page are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG) and agree with the description of Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 246-259).

docs.title: Subject – verb – object
docs.text:
The basic order is subject + verb + objects and complements:

Subject Verb Object(s) Hala cɔaw halataalaa a lɛŋnden “God created the heavens and the earth” Gen 1:1 Kain del Abɛl pɔmbɔ ndɔ coo “Cain fell upon his brother Abel” Gen 4:8

The object follows the verb directly; then comes the complement of place or manner: mó dimul nda aa “he said to them” (verb + object + speech) Gen 1:28.

docs.title: The resumptive pronoun after the subject
docs.text:
When the subject is a noun of a class other than o, it is taken up again by its class pronoun just before the verb (Childs 1995, p. 257-258):

  • Lɛŋnden le va tulumasaa “the earth was formless” Gen 1:2 (class len → le);
  • Ɲumma bɛndu-bɛnduan ma va matoalaa “the great waters were…” Gen 1:2 (class an → ma);
  • mí vannda a va kɔlan “and the people were walking” Luke 7:12 (persons plur. → a).

With a singular noun of the o class, the verb follows directly: Mí vanalanɔɔ mulul ndu aa “And the woman answered him” Gen 3:2.

Rule

Noun subject (except class o) + class pronoun + verb: Lɛŋnden le va, kobilan la va. The pronoun is written as a separate word.

docs.title: Position of other elements
docs.text:
Element Position Example Determiners, adjectives, numbers after the noun pee bɛndoo, kobio ho, simlacia nda yáá Noun complement (possessor) after the noun lɛŋnde Esipte len “the land of Egypt” Gen 13:10 Relative clause after the noun kɔngɔ vesɛi fula-o Gen 1:10 Negation le / te end of clause I sínà le 1 Sam 17:55 Particle ni, yɛ end of clause Paale taselen le yɔŋnun nden ni Gen 1:5 Ideophone end of clause Diimandɔɔ idiiyo púŋ Gen 21:14 Time expression at the start or end of the sentence O kon kɔɔli, mí… “After that…” Gen 2:8

Kisiei thus places the determiner after the noun and the object after the verb; only the prepositions a, o, le come before their noun, most relations of place being expressed by a postposition (o nakɔɔ ho nin).

Subject Resumptive pronoun Verb Objects (object, then place) End of clause Lɛŋnden le va tulumasaa · Gen 1:2 Hala · cɔaw halataalaa a lɛŋnden · Gen 1:1 I · sínà · le 1 Sam 17:55 The slots of the simple sentence. The resumptive pronoun follows a noun subject that is not of the o class; negation and particles close the clause.

docs.title: Focus
docs.text: To put an element in focus, it is placed at the start of the sentence and the sentence ends with the particle ni: Nda yɔŋnun kuubaa cɔvaa masindɛa ni “It was they who became the heroes” Gen 6:4. A focused subject takes the independent form of the pronoun (Nda, Ndu, Ya); see Personal pronouns.

docs.title: Adverbs and ideophones
docs.text: Adverbs are invariable; they are usually placed after the verb and its objects, at the end of the sentence or just before the negation (Keita 1979, p. 116). The forms and examples below are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG).

docs.title: Adverbs of time
docs.text: Word Meaning Example (Bible) hau today, now kandɔɔ hau “from now on” Gen 4:11 nihau now, this time Má cè nihau paa “This at last is bone” Gen 2:23 sunsun now, right away Lelan sunsun “Now therefore” Gen 21:23 siɔdii tomorrow Siɔdii idii “tomorrow morning” Gen 19:2 idii, idiiyo in the morning, early Diimandɔɔ idiiyo púŋ “early the next morning” Gen 21:14 icɔllo / ipalaa evening / morning, day Mí ɲɔɔ yɔŋnun icɔllo a ipalaa “There was evening and there was morning” Gen 1:5 ɲinasiaŋ next year boondei he ɲinasiaŋ-ndo “at this time next year” Gen 17:21 le fɛɛn a fɛɛn for ever o co vannɔn yoomu le fɛɛn a fɛɛn “he would live for ever” Gen 3:22 few never (with the negation) Ɲɛm mun pɛnginin tosanndo le few “these things will never cease” Gen 8:22

docs.title: Adverbs of place
docs.text: Word Meaning Example (Bible) nanu here muungu nanu “will come back here” Gen 15:16 lon there, over there má cal lon “they settled there” Gen 11:31 lecoo on top, above ɲɛ-ɲɛ ve lecoo le “there was nothing on it” Gen 1:2 labɛngu underneath, below 1 Kgs 7:34

docs.title: Adverbs of quantity and degree
docs.text:
Word Meaning Example (Bible) taw very, much n naŋ taw “it was very good” Gen 1:31 kpow completely, all Mɛɛ Hala cii baala kon tosa kpow Gen 2:2 faw all, completely visia bɛndua a à pɔmbɔa faw Gen 8:17

See also the indefinites.

docs.title: Ideophones
docs.text:
Ideophones are expressive words that depict a sound, a manner, an intensity or a visual impression; they follow the verb or adjective they reinforce and are often reduplicated. They form a class of their own, with a particular prosody, described in detail for Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 132-140). Examples from the Bible:

  • idiiyo púŋ “early in the morning, at dawn” Gen 21:14;
  • mà faŋan … few-few “go away at once!” Gen 12:19;
  • hoeyii ken niinu … kpɛŋ “these locusts covered (the land) entirely” Exod 10:13;
  • o puiyaa tɛi-tɛi “well watered everywhere” Gen 13:10.

Spelling rules

  • Adverbs are written as separate words: kandɔɔ hau, n naŋ taw.
  • A reduplicated ideophone is written with a hyphen: few-few, tɛi-tɛi; the Bible often marks the tone on it (púŋ).
  • Fixed expressions are written as separate words: le fɛɛn a fɛɛn.

1979 usage

The 1979 description gives lists of adverbs of place, time, manner and quantity in the old orthography (kpèèlun, levil, nanu, lon, lebèngu; lapöm, haw, siödii, diilèn, sunsun; taw, faw, tyapo…) (Keita 1979, p. 116). Most of them are found in the Bible in their current form (nanu, lon, hau, sunsun, diilɛn, taw, faw).

docs.title: Invariable words
docs.text:
These words do not change form for class or number.

  • Adverbs and ideophones;
  • Particles: ni, aa, yɛ, politeness -ndɔ, pila, bɛɛ…;
  • Prepositions, postpositions and conjunctions: a, o … nin, kani, te … pɛ…;
  • Interjections, greetings and responses.

docs.title: Interjections, greetings and responses
docs.text:
Interjections express an emotion, a call or a response; they are set off from the rest of the sentence by a comma or an exclamation mark. The forms below are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG).

Word Use Example (Bible) Oi yes Oi, i yeema “Yes, I will” Gen 24:58 Ɛ-ɛ no Ɛ-ɛ, n nɔla mì n de “No, we may eat” Gen 3:2 Mbaa answer to a call (“yes?”) Mbaa. Nɔm nɛ̀ɛ́-nɛ̀? “Yes? Who are you?” Gen 27:18 isɛ greeting Pua isɛ “Greetings, father” Gen 27:18 balika thank you mí mel ndu balika “I thanked him” Gen 24:48 Ɛ̀ɛ̀ astonishment, admiration Ɛ̀ɛ̀ hɛ́ɛ̀! “Ah! Here at last…” Gen 2:23 Yàá surprise Yàá Mɛlɛka co o fondaa ho! “Surely the Lord is in this place!” Gen 28:16

Southern Kissi adds to greetings an emphatic particle ó (ìsɛ̀ó, ìdììyó), which makes them warmer (Childs 1995, p. 144-145). In the Bible, idii means “in the morning, early” (Siɔdii idii “tomorrow morning” Gen 19:2; idii a icɔl “morning and evening” Exod 27:20); its use as a leave-taking formula still needs to be checked.

Spelling rules

  • A reduplicated interjection takes a hyphen: Ɛ-ɛ.
  • The tone marks on interjections (Ɛ̀ɛ̀, Yàá) are written as in the Bible.
  • The greeting is written as two words: Pua isɛ.

1979 usage

The 1979 description cites kanikokoe (joy), se (call), kpoki (surprise), kpöö (disgust) and taa (Keita 1979, p. 119); these forms do not appear in the Bible.

docs.title: Particles
docs.text: Particles are small words with no lexical meaning of their own, which mark a grammatical relation or a nuance. The forms and examples below are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG), compared with the 1979 description (Keita 1979, p. 117-118) and with that of Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 142-145).

docs.title: Sentence particles
docs.text:
Particle Function Example (Bible) ni affirmation, identification, focus (“it is…”) Paale taselen le yɔŋnun nden ni “That was the first day” Gen 1:5; Hoo co masa Yuifia ni “This is the king of the Jews” Luke 23:38 le / te negation, at the end of the clause see Negation yɛ ends a content question, after the verb Kuɛɛ nɛ n co yɛ “Where are you?” Gen 3:9; see Interrogatives aa introduces reported speech Mí Hala dimi aa “And God said:” Gen 1:3 pɛ closes the condition opened by te te o de pɛ kɔmnde yɔm kon Gen 3:22

The particle ni ends the sentence that identifies or focuses an element; in the corresponding negative sentence, it is replaced by the final negation (see Negation). Southern Kissi has the same focus particle ní (Childs 1995, p. 124).

docs.title: Politeness particle: -ndɔ, -yɔ, -lɔ
docs.text:
Attached to the verb of an order or a request, this particle softens the demand (“then, please”); it is written with a hyphen and takes the form -ndɔ after a nasal, -yɔ after i, -lɔ after l:

  • La yaŋ-ndɔ nilan “Listen to me, then” Gen 4:23;
  • la tuei-yɔ ɲɛ ya co niaa dimul-lo “hear what I am telling you” Gen 4:23;
  • La mɛi-yɔ “Wait, please” Gen 18:5.

Southern Kissi has the same politeness particle (wɔ, variants ndɔ, lɔ) after the imperative and the hortative (Childs 1995, p. 144). The Bible also uses -lɔ in other contexts (ndóò vil-lɔ … le Gen 2:5), whose meaning remains to be clarified (see the open questions).

docs.title: Noun phrase particles
docs.text:
Placed just after the noun or pronoun, they specify its scope (Keita 1979, p. 117-118):

Particle Meaning Example (Bible) pila self (himself) Niaa pila bɛɛ la sina “you yourselves know” Gen 31:6 bɛɛ also; even yɔmnde bɛɛ fulá “let the trees also come forth” Gen 1:11 kpé only, alone nɔm pilɛ kpé “you alone” Gen 7:1 kpeekpei exactly, precisely fonda … kpeekpei “the very place” Gen 13:4 daama only latámán kɛmɛ lehiɔɔlu daama “only four hundred (shekels)” Gen 23:15 vɛlɛ again, also (after the verb) Mí Hala dimi vɛlɛ aa “God said again” Gen 1:6

vɛlɛ is the only one of these particles that is placed after the verb (Keita 1979, p. 118).

Spelling rules

  • Particles are written separately: ya pila, nɔm pilɛ kpé, dimi vɛlɛ.
  • Only the politeness particle is attached to the verb, with a hyphen: yaŋ-ndɔ, tuei-yɔ.

1979 usage

The 1979 description also cites kuani, tuun and sii “only” and pɛn (Keita 1979, p. 117), which do not appear, or hardly appear, in the Bible.

docs.title: Prepositions, postpositions and conjunctions
docs.text: The forms and examples on this page are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG); they are compared with the 1979 description (Keita 1979, p. 117-119) and with that of Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 129-131, 141-142).

docs.title: Prepositions
docs.text:
Kisiei has only three simple prepositions, like Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 129):

Preposition Meaning Example (Bible) a with, by means of; and vanaa bɛndua a à pɔmbɔa “great and small”; cɔwnun a yɔmnde “made of wood” Deut 4:28 o at, in, on (place, time) o paale ŋɔmmɛwndɔlen coo “on the seventh day” Gen 2:2 le for, because of le dioo “to eat” Gen 3:11; Le hee “because of that” Gen 2:21

Watch out for homonyms: o the preposition and o the pronoun “he, she”; le “for” and le the negative particle; a “with, and” and a the pronoun “you, they”.

docs.title: Circumpositions: o … postposition
docs.text:
To specify a location, the noun is framed by o and a postposition placed after it (Childs 1995, p. 129-131):

Construction Meaning Example (Bible) o … nin in o nakɔɔ ho nin “in this garden” Gen 2:16 o … coo on o mɛnndan coo “on the waters” Gen 1:2 o … lo at the home of, to (a person) o vanapɔnɔɔ lo “to the man” Gen 2:19 o … ba bɛngu in the hands of, by Mɛlɛka o ba bɛngu “by the Lord, from the hand of the Lord” Gen 4:1 … tɛɛn between, among mɛnndan sɛiyo tɛɛn “in the midst of the waters” Gen 1:6 … ikɛi with, beside Noe ikɛi “to Noah” Gen 7:15 … kɔɔli after, behind O kon kɔɔli “after that” Gen 2:8

The 1979 description likewise gives o … lo “at the home of” and o … nin “in” (Keita 1979, p. 119).

Spelling rule

o and the postposition are written as separate words: o nakɔɔ ho nin, o mɛnndan coo. When a relative clause ends with the postposition, the class ending is attached to it with a hyphen: coo-o, nin-ndan (see Relative clauses).

docs.title: Coordinating conjunctions
docs.text:
Word Meaning Example (Bible) a and (between nouns) halataalaa a lɛŋnden “the heavens and the earth” Gen 1:1 nda and (between names of people) Moise nda Aarɔn “Moses and Aaron” Exod 5:1 kɛ but Kɛ mí Mɛlɛka mulul ndu aa “But the Lord answered him” Num 12:14 ɔ́ɔ̀ or (else), is it that Kɛ ɔ́ɔ̀ saa téndé… “but where is the lamb…?” Gen 22:7 te kon te or else, otherwise te kon te Gen 24:21 mi and (then); see Tense, aspect, mood Mí Hala dimi aa Gen 1:3 lelan that is why, therefore Lelan, vanapɔnɔɔ faŋannin fuɲa ndɔ “That is why a man will leave his father” Gen 2:24 nduyɛ however, indeed Kɛ nduyɛ, la dia vision… “Only, you shall not eat the flesh…” Gen 9:4

nda links names of people or animals, a other nouns (Keita 1979, p. 119): Mí Bɛnyamɛn nda Hakub va baalaa tosaa “Benjamin and Hasshub were working” Neh 3:23.

docs.title: Subordinating conjunctions
docs.text:
Word Meaning Example (Bible) kani because, for kani o falun… “for she was taken…” Gen 2:23 le tùú because, since Le tùú n cɛl sɔɛi laa nɔm-nde “Because you listened to your wife” Gen 3:17 haliko so that haliko mi la va baloo dɔwnɔnndo “so that it may be your food” Gen 1:29 te … pɛ if, when te o de pɛ kɔmnde yɔm kon “if he eats of the fruit of this tree” Gen 3:22 mɛɛ … yɛ as, in the way that mɛɛ súúla ndɔlan la co yɛ “according to their kinds” Gen 1:11 Mɛɛ when (narrative) Mɛɛ Hala cii baala kon tosa kpow “When God had finished his work” Gen 2:2 Tuma at the time when, when Tuma Mɛlɛka Hala cɔw halataalaa a lɛŋnden-ndo “When the Lord God made the heavens and the earth” Gen 2:4 maa that (after say, see, know) mó ca maa n naŋ taw “he saw that it was very good” Gen 1:31 aa (introduces speech) Mí Hala dimi aa: «…» Gen 1:3 háá until, up to háá o kpóŋndán “up to the ceiling” 1 Kgs 6:15 hali even; even if hali billo bɛɛ ndóò vil-lɔ le “not even the plants had sprung up yet” Gen 2:5

The condition is built with te at the start and pɛ after the verb of the clause: Te … pɛ. Southern Kissi uses the same construction (tè … pɛ́), as well as àà “that”, màà “that, as”, mɛ̀ɛ́ … (yɛ́) “when, as” (Childs 1995, p. 141-142). The 1979 description also cites hanikpe “so that”, baw and fuule “because” (Keita 1979, p. 119), which are absent or very rare in the Bible.

Spelling rules

  • aa introducing speech is followed by a colon and quotation marks: dimi aa: «…» (see Punctuation).
  • te “if” opens the clause and pɛ follows its verb; do not confuse them with the final negation te.
  • háá “until” carries its accents, to distinguish it from haa “these”.

docs.title: Derived verbs
docs.text:
From a basic verb, Kisiei forms new verbs by suffixation or by changing the stem. The 1979 description distinguishes four kinds: reflexive verbs, reciprocal verbs, verbs “of help” (for someone's benefit) and verbs of repetition (Keita 1979, p. 92-94). The description of Southern Kissi speaks of verbal extensions and also counts four: causative, benefactive, middle and plural (Childs 1995, p. 171-194). The two classifications largely overlap; the forms and examples below are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG).

Derivation Form Base → derived (Bible) Benefactive (“for, to someone”) -l, -ul dimi “say” → dimul “say to”; tosa “do” → tosal “do for”; soli “offer” → solul “offer to”; sɛva “write” → sɛval “write to” Middle, reflexive, passive -n, -nun, -nndo cɔm “show” → cɔmnun “show oneself, appear”; tosa → tosan “be done, happen”; pulun / pulɔnndo “wash oneself” Reciprocal -an yil “greet” → yilan “greet each other” Causative -i- hiow “pass” → hivia “make pass”; vesa “be dry” → veesiaa “dry up (something)” Plural, intensive long vowel + -uu kumbu “cover” → kuumbuu “cover over (completely)”; tɛɛmbuu “destroy”

docs.title: Benefactive: -l, -ul
docs.text:
The benefactive shows that the action is done for or addressed to someone, who becomes the direct object:

  • mó dimul nda aa “and he said to them” Gen 1:28 (from dimi “say”);
  • ɲɛ Ham po ndɔ tosal ndu-o “what his son Ham had done to him” Gen 9:24;
  • mó solul Mɛlɛka sálàá “and he offered a sacrifice to the Lord” Gen 4:3.

The long form doubles the l: sɛvallo “write for someone” Judg 8:14, as the 1979 description already notes (sèvallo, mandallo) (Keita 1979, p. 93). The Southern Kissi benefactive has the same form -(l)ul (Childs 1995, p. 178-184).

docs.title: Middle: -n, -nun
docs.text:
The middle turns the action back towards the subject: a reflexive meaning (“oneself”), a passive one (“be done”) or an intransitive one:

  • Mí Mɛlɛka cɔmnun Abram “The Lord appeared to Abram” Gen 12:7 (from cɔm “show”);
  • Mí ɲɔɔ tosan lende “And it was so” Gen 1:7;
  • yɔŋ vɔɔndo va tosanndo “evil was being done” Gen 6:11;
  • le pulɔnndo “to wash herself” Exod 2:5.

The long form of the middle ends in -nndo (tosanndo, pulɔnndo, pilanndo). The 1979 description presents these verbs as reflexive pronominal verbs in -ndo and -nɔnndo (susanndo “rub oneself”, diinɔnndo “kill oneself”) (Keita 1979, p. 92-93); for Southern Kissi, the middle (-nuŋ) is the only extension that carries a tone of its own (Childs 1995, p. 184-190).

docs.title: Reciprocal: -an
docs.text: The reciprocal expresses a mutual action: Má yilan “They greeted each other” 2 Kgs 10:15. The 1979 description gives -anndo and -lanndo for the long form (yilanndo “greet each other”, vaalanndo “farm for each other”) (Keita 1979, p. 93); these long forms do not appear in the Bible.

docs.title: Causative: -i-
docs.text:
The causative adds or inserts an i and often changes the stem vowel; it means “cause to do, make”:

  • hiow “pass” → hivia “make pass”: vana hivia isɔɔ “an interpreter (one who makes words pass across)” Gen 42:23;
  • vesa “be dry” → veesiaa “dry up (something)” Gen 41:6.

The 1979 description classes these verbs among the verbs of repetition formed with the infix i (veesaa → veesiaa “make dry”, hiovöö → hivioo “make pass”) (Keita 1979, p. 94). For Southern Kissi, the causative is also -i, and some verbs have the same form in the causative and the plural (Childs 1995, p. 175-178, 190).

docs.title: Plural: long vowel and -uu
docs.text:
The plural indicates a repeated action, one affecting several objects or one done by several subjects; it lengthens the stem vowel and ends the verb in -uu (Childs 1995, p. 190-194):

  • kumbu “cover” (Yondoo fulá mò kumbu kɔngɔ vesɛiyo Gen 1:11) → kuumbuu (má kuumbuu doma bɛndu kon ndu coo “they spread the garment over him” Gen 9:23);
  • tɛɛmbuu “destroy, wipe out” Gen 6:17.

docs.title: Reduplication
docs.text:
Reduplicating the verb expresses repetition or spreading of the action; it is written as one word or with a hyphen: misimisi “devour” Gen 41:20. The 1979 description gives kèsikesio “arrange”, kilikilio “cut into small pieces” (Keita 1979, p. 94).

Spelling rules

  • Derivational suffixes are written joined to the verb: dimul, cɔmnun, yilan, kuumbuu.
  • The derived verb keeps the spelling of the base verb, except where a vowel change is actually pronounced (hiow → hivia).

docs.title: The verb
docs.text:
The Kisiei verb does not change for person: it is the subject pronoun that shows who is acting. What varies is the stem (long or short form, changed vowel), the tone, and the small words around it: the auxiliaries co and va, the suffix -nin, the negative particle le / te.

This chapter describes:

  • Stems and groups: long form and short forms, regular verbs and vowel-alternating verbs;
  • Tense, aspect, mood: perfective, habitual, progressive, future, narrative, subjunctive, imperative;
  • Negation: the final particle and the negative stem;
  • Derived verbs: benefactive, middle, reciprocal, causative, plural.

The conjugation tables are in the Reference.

docs.title: Negation
docs.text: Negation is marked by a particle at the end of the clause, le or te, and, for many verbs, by a change of stem (Keita 1979, p. 72, 94-104). The same structure is described for Southern Kissi: a final particle le and changes of tone and vowel on the verb (Childs 1995, p. 222-223, 260-264). The rules and examples below are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG).

docs.title: The final particle: le or te
docs.text:
The particle is placed at the end of the negated clause, after the objects and complements:

  • I sínà le “I do not know” 1 Sam 17:55;
  • o di ɲɛdiaa le, o kol vɛlɛ le “he ate no food and did not drink either” Exod 34:28.

It takes the form te when the word before it ends in a nasal consonant (n, m, ŋ) or in l; after a vowel or w, it stays le. In the Bible, te follows a nasal more than 2,600 times and l more than 360 times, and le is never found after these consonants. The 1979 description mentions only the nasals (Keita 1979, p. 72); the description of Southern Kissi gives te after any consonant (Childs 1995, p. 142-143).

  • I mel nɔm te “I will not let you (go)” Gen 32:27;
  • hali pilanndo bɛɛ la pilan te “do not even touch it” Gen 3:3;
  • i kuenin te “I will not go” Judg 4:8;
  • n fúlà lɛ ndu o hɔl te “you shall not appear before him” (after l) Gen 43:5;
  • ndóò ci lɛ taw le “he could no longer see at all” (after w) Gen 48:10.

Spelling rule

  • Write te after n, m, ŋ or l, and le after a vowel or w: I mel nɔm te, o hɔl te, but o kol vɛlɛ le, taw le.
  • The particle is always written as a separate word, at the end of the negated clause, before the comma or full stop.
flowchart LR
    W["Last letter of the word<br>before the particle"] --> Q{"<i>n, m, ŋ</i><br>or <i>l</i>?"}
    Q -- yes --> T["<i>te</i><br><i>I mel nɔm te</i>"]
    Q -- "no (vowel or <i>w</i>)" --> L["<i>le</i><br><i>o kol vɛlɛ le</i>"]
le or te? It depends on the last letter before the particle.

docs.title: Negative stem
docs.text:
Alternating verbs take a stem with a changed vowel in the negative (see Stems and groups):

Affirmative Negative a mam “you laughed” I mem te “I did not laugh” Gen 18:15 mal “leave” I mel nɔm te Gen 32:27 de “eat” o di ɲɛdiaa le Exod 34:28 kɔa “go” te naa n kue … le Gen 43:3 
flowchart LR
    A1["<i>a</i> · <i>mam</i>"] --> B1["<i>e</i> · <i>mem</i>"]
    A2["<i>u</i> · <i>vu</i>"] --> B2["<i>i</i> · <i>vi</i>"]
    A3["<i>o</i> · <i>tol</i>"] --> B3["<i>u</i> · <i>tul</i>"]
    A4["<i>io, ia</i> · <i>dia</i>"] --> B4["<i>i, e</i> · <i>di</i>"]
    A5["<i>ɔa</i> · <i>kɔa</i>"] --> B5["<i>ue</i> · <i>kue</i>"]
The vowel changes of the negative stem, affirmative on the left, negative on the right (see Stems and groups).

docs.title: Progressive and “to be” in the past: ve
docs.text: In the negative, the past auxiliary va becomes ve: ɲɛ-ɲɛ ve lecoo le “there was nothing on it” Gen 1:2; vanaa … ve cɛinin te “the people were not in the house” Gen 39:11. Southern Kissi has the same wa / we alternation (Childs 1995, p. 234).

docs.title: Future: -nin … le / te
docs.text: The negative future keeps the suffix -nin and, for alternating verbs, the vowel of the negative: o dinin ndu tɔnɔ le “he will not eat of it (its fruit)” Deut 28:30; i kɛɛnin te “I will not refuse” 1 Kgs 2:20.

docs.title: Prohibition (negative imperative)
docs.text: The negative imperative uses the habitual stem and the final particle: La dia le “do not eat of it” Gen 3:3, La suunda le “You shall not commit adultery” Exod 20:14.

docs.title: “Not yet”, “nothing”, “nobody”
docs.text:
• vɔ … le “not yet”: Mɛlɛka Hala ndóò tuisi vɔ piɔɔ … le Gen 2:5;
  • ɲɛ-ɲɛ … le “nothing”: ɲɛ-ɲɛ ve lecoo le Gen 1:2;
  • vana-vana … le “nobody”: vana-vana ve lasiɛmbu … le Gen 2:25.

docs.title: Negating an identity
docs.text:
To negate “it is X”, co and the final particle are used, where the affirmative uses the particle ni: Hoo co masa Yuifia ni “this is the king of the Jews” Luke 23:38 versus O co dɛnɛ vana bɛnda le tosa le “it is not a thing that ought to be done” Gen 20:9. In this construction, Southern Kissi puts the noun's class pronoun before it (Childs 1995, p. 261-262); this point still needs to be checked for the Kisiei of Guinea.

1979 usage

The le / te rule is described in 1979 for the nasals only (“le is realised as te when the final sound of the word before it is nasal”) (Keita 1979, p. 72); the Bible extends it to l. The 1979 tables also give the negative of each tense (I tyo kolö le, I kol te, I kolnin te) (Keita 1979, p. 96-104).

docs.title: Long form and short forms
docs.text:
Every verb has a long form (called the “infinitive” in 1979 (Keita 1979, p. 90-91)), ending in a long vowel or a class ending, and one or more short forms (stems):

Long form Short form Meaning tosaa tosa do, make malɔɔ mal leave, let go kolɔɔ kol drink dioo de, dia, dio, di eat kɔlan kɔa, kɔɛ, kɔ, kue go, leave cɛlɔɔ cɛl accept

The long form is used after the auxiliaries co and va (progressive aspect) and as a verbal noun: o va kelaa “he was walking” Gen 6:9; dɛnɛ vaa nuaa tosaa “to do such a thing” Gen 11:6. The short forms are used for the other tenses and moods and for the negative (see Tense, aspect, mood).

The long form is in fact a verbal noun of the o class; it ends like a noun (-aa, -ɔɔ, -oo, -ndo…). Southern Kissi likewise forms the verbal noun with the suffix -o (Childs 1995, p. 202-203).

docs.title: Regular verbs and alternating verbs
docs.text:
The 1979 description sorts verbs into four groups according to the number of different stems (Keita 1979, p. 101-104). For Southern Kissi, a simpler distinction is made between regular verbs, whose vowel does not change, and irregular verbs, whose vowel changes with tense, aspect and polarity; tense is marked first of all by tone (Childs 1995, p. 219-224). The texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG) confirm these two types:

flowchart LR
    subgraph REG["Regular verb: the vowel does not change"]
        T["<i>tosaa</i>"] --> T1["<i>tosa</i> perfective"]
        T --> T2["<i>tosanin</i> future"]
        T --> T3["<i>tosa le</i> negative"]
    end
    subgraph ALT["Alternating verbs: the vowel changes"]
        M["<i>malɔɔ</i>"] --> M1["<i>mal</i> affirmative"]
        M --> M2["<i>mel</i> negative"]
        D["<i>dioo</i>"] --> D1["<i>de</i> perfective, narrative"]
        D --> D2["<i>dia</i> habitual, prohibition"]
        D --> D3["<i>dio</i> near future"]
        D --> D4["<i>di</i> negative"]
    end
One stem for the whole verb, or stems that change their vowel.

docs.title: Regular verbs (1st group of 1979)
docs.text:
The vowel stays the same throughout; only the ending changes:

Long form Perfective Future Negative tosaa tosa tosanin tosa le cɛlɔɔ cɛl cɛlnin

Examples: Mí ɲɔɔ tosan lende “And it was so” Gen 1:7; ɲɛ-ɲɛ nɔla lɛ mò kuuna nda … tosa le “nothing will stop them from doing…” Gen 11:6.

docs.title: Vowel-alternating verbs (2nd to 4th group of 1979)
docs.text:
The stem vowel changes, above all in the negative:

Meaning Affirmative Negative Example (Bible) leave mal mel I mel nɔm te “I will not let you go” Gen 32:27 laugh mam mem I mem te “I did not laugh”; a mam “you laughed” Gen 18:15 eat de, dia di o di ɲɛdiaa le “he did not eat” Exod 34:28 go kɔa, kɔɛ kue te naa n kue … le “if we do not go” Gen 43:3

These changes follow a few regular patterns, found across all the verbs in the lexicon:

Change Examples (affirmative / negative) a → e mam / mem, mal / mel, ca / ce u → i vu / vi, hun / hin o → u tol / tul, kow / kuw io, ia → i, e hiow / hiw, dia / di, pial / pel ɔa → ue kɔa / kue

Example: Taa yeema mà vi le “if you do not want to die” Gen 19:17 (vu “die”). The description of Southern Kissi reports the same kind of vowel alternation in its irregular verbs (Childs 1995, p. 220-221, 241-244).

The negative future keeps the vowel of the negative: dinin “will not eat” Deut 28:30, kuenin te “I will not go” Judg 4:8.

docs.title: The forms of “eat” and “go”
docs.text:
The most irregular verbs have four stems. Their use in the Bible:

eat go Use Example long form dioo kɔlan progressive, verbal noun le dioo “to eat” perfective, subordinate de kɔa narrative, condition, relative te o de pɛ “if he eats” Gen 3:22; má kɔa yondoo nin “they went to the fields” Gen 4:8 habitual, prohibition dia kɔɛ habit, negative imperative, subjunctive La dia le “do not eat of it” Gen 3:3; mì n kɔɛ “let us go” Gen 4:8 short stem dio kɔ near future, serial verb n co ndu dio “you will eat of it” Gen 2:17; N kɔ delnun ndu coo “let us go and fall upon him” Gen 37:20 negative di kue negation o di ɲɛdiaa le Exod 34:28 future dianin kɔanin future nda dianin “they will eat” Exod 12:7

Spelling rules

  • Write each stem as it is pronounced: mal / mel, dia / di; do not “regularise” it.
  • The future suffix -nin is written joined to the stem: tosanin, dianin, kuenin.
  • The long form is written with its long vowel or its ending: tosaa, malɔɔ, dioo.

1979 usage

The 1979 description names the stems R1 to R4 and gives, for each group, a table of their use (Keita 1979, p. 101-104), as well as a lexicon of verbs sorted by group (Keita 1979, p. 110-118). These tables are in the old orthography (Dioo : de, dia, dio, di; Kölan : köè, köa, kö, koe). The distribution of stems found in the Bible broadly agrees, but the Bible writes kɔa for the narrative perfective and kɔɛ after mì, where 1979 gives köè for the past and köa for the habitual; this point still needs to be checked with speakers.

docs.title: Tense, aspect and mood
docs.text:
The Kisiei verb is not conjugated for person: the subject is carried by the pronoun. Tense, aspect and mood are expressed by:

  1. the tone of the verb and of the pronoun (rarely marked in writing);
  2. the choice of stem (long or short form, changed vowel; see Stems and groups);
  3. auxiliaries placed before the verb (co, va);
  4. the suffix -nin;
  5. lengthening of the subject pronoun (ndóò, yáà).

Aspect matters more than tense: the first contrast is between the completed action (perfective) and the ongoing or habitual action (Childs 1995, p. 219-222). The forms and examples on this page are drawn from the texts of the Kisiei Bible (BKG); they are compared with the 1979 description (Keita 1979, p. 94-101) and with that of Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 218-245).

past future now Remote past ndóò hiow Past progressive o va kelaa Perfective I tuei Present progressive i co hunɔɔ Near future n co ndu dio Future tosanin The verb forms placed on a time line. The past progressive lasts up to a moment in the past.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Form Construction Example (Bible) Perfective pronoun + short stem I tuei “I have heard” Gen 27:6 Habitual pronoun + stem (different tone) o co kɛndɛ “he is well” Gen 29:6 Present progressive co + long form i co hunɔɔ “I am coming, I am going to” Gen 6:17 Past progressive va + long form o va kelaa “he was walking” Gen 6:9 Near future co + short stem n co ndu dio “you will eat of it” Gen 2:17 Future stem + -nin I tuisinin nɔm “I will put on you” Gen 3:16 Remote past lengthened pronoun + stem Kɛwvo ndóò hiow “the serpent was more (cunning)” Gen 3:1 Future in the past, conditional lengthened pronoun + stem-nin mɛɛ ndóò kenin nda diolan yɛ “what he would call them” Gen 2:19 Narrative (“and then…”) mí / mó / má + stem Mí Hala dimi aa “And God said” Gen 1:3 Subjunctive mì / mò / mà + stem Yondoo fulá mò kumbu kɔngɔ vesɛiyo “let the vegetation come forth and cover the earth” Gen 1:11 Imperative stem (+ la in the plural) La náŋ ipúlú, la kuí “Be fruitful, multiply” Gen 1:28 
flowchart LR
    S["What is to<br>be expressed?"] --> G1["An ongoing<br>action"]
    S --> G2["A future<br>action"]
    S --> G3["A sequence<br>with <i>mi</i>"]
    S --> G4["A completed<br>or habitual fact"]
    G1 -- now --> P1["Present progressive: <i>co</i> + long form<br><i>i co hunɔɔ</i>"]
    G1 -- "in the past" --> P2["Past progressive: <i>va</i> + long form<br><i>o va kelaa</i>"]
    G2 -- "near, certain" --> F1["Near future: <i>co</i> + short stem<br><i>n co ndu dio</i>"]
    G2 -- "promise, prediction" --> F2["Future: stem + <i>-nin</i><br><i>tosanin</i>"]
    G3 -- narrative --> R1["Narrative: <i>mí</i> / <i>mó</i> / <i>má</i> + stem<br><i>Mí Hala dimi aa</i>"]
    G3 -- "purpose, wish" --> R2["Subjunctive: <i>mì</i> / <i>mò</i> / <i>mà</i> + stem<br><i>mò vel naa</i>"]
    G4 -- "remote past" --> PR["Remote past: lengthened pronoun + stem<br><i>ndóò</i>, <i>yáà</i>"]
    G4 -- otherwise --> A["Perfective or habitual: pronoun + stem<br><i>I tuei</i>"]
Choosing the verb form. The imperative and negation are covered below.

docs.title: Perfective and habitual
docs.text: The short form of the verb, without an auxiliary, expresses the completed action: I tuei “I have heard”, a mam “you laughed” Gen 18:15. The same form also expresses habit or a general truth; the two are distinguished by tone (low tone for the habitual, high tone for the perfective) (Keita 1979, p. 95), which the description of Southern Kissi confirms (Childs 1995, p. 224-227). The Bible does not mark this tone: the context decides.

docs.title: The progressive: co and va
docs.text:
The auxiliary co “to be (in the act of)” followed by the long form expresses an action in progress; in the past, va is used:

  • i co hunɔɔ mɛmma bɛnduan soli “I am going to bring the flood” Gen 6:17;
  • Kɔl Hala-o va o pɛɛngaa o mɛmma man coo “the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters” Gen 1:2.

co and va are also the forms of the verb to be: Lɛŋnden le va tulumasaa “the earth was formless” Gen 1:2. In the negative, va becomes ve: ɲɛ-ɲɛ ve lecoo le “there was nothing on it” Gen 1:2. Southern Kissi has the same wa / we contrast (Childs 1995, p. 233-234).

docs.title: The future
docs.text:
Two constructions exist side by side:

  1. co + short stem (near or certain future): n co ndu dio “(the day) you eat of it” Gen 2:17. This is the ordinary future construction in Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 234-235); the 1979 description calls it the futur immédiat (immediate future) (Keita 1979, p. 95).
  2. stem + -nin (future, promise, prediction; futur lointain, distant future, in 1979): I tuisinin nɔm sangalan coo “I will multiply your pains” Gen 3:16, I yɔngunin cuavaa nɔmaa imamaa lɛŋnden nden “I will give this land to your offspring” Gen 12:7.

In the negative, -nin keeps the vowel of the negative: i kuenin te “I will not go” Judg 4:8, i kɛɛnin te “I will not refuse” 1 Kgs 2:20.

docs.title: The lengthened pronoun: remote past and conditional
docs.text:
Lengthening the subject pronoun, with a high tone, places the action or state in a remote past: “he was (once)”, “he had”. Southern Kissi has exactly the same device (óó kòl, ndóó) (Childs 1995, p. 231-232). The Bible writes the lengthened independent pronoun as one word, with its tones:

Person Form Example 1st sing. yáà te yáà de pɛ “if I had eaten” Lev 10:19 3rd sing. ndóò yɔmndo ndu pilɛ bɛɛ ndóò vil-lɔ … le “no tree had yet sprung up” Gen 2:5 3rd plur. ndáà ɲɛm vanaa kan ndáà manda “the provisions these people had kept” Gen 14:11

With -nin, the same form expresses the future in the past or the conditional: mɛɛ ndóò kenin nda diolan yɛ “what he would call them” Gen 2:19; ndóò venin a siɛmbula lan le “would she not be covered with shame?” Num 12:14.

The 1979 description classes these forms under a conditional mood marked by lengthening of the pronoun (Ii kolnin, Ii va kolöö) (Keita 1979, p. 99-100).

docs.title: Narrative and subjunctive: mi + pronoun
docs.text:
The word mi “and (then)” combines with the subject pronoun: mó (mi + o), má (mi + a), mí n, mí la. The tone of this form is grammatical, and the Bible marks it:

  • high tone: completed action, the sequence of the narrative: mó yaa nda “and he brought them” Gen 2:19, má kuumbuu “and they covered” Gen 9:23;
  • low tone: non-completed action: purpose, wish, expected consequence (subjunctive): mò vel naa “(that he may be) in our likeness” Gen 1:26, mì n kɔɛ “so that we may go” Gen 4:8.

Southern Kissi has the same forms (mbo = mi + o, ma, mila, miŋ) and the same tone contrast (mbó kwɛ̀ “then he left”, mbò kwɛ̀ “then he leaves”) (Childs 1995, p. 239-240). In 1979, the subjunctive is described with maa + pronoun (Keita 1979, p. 100); the Bible uses maa “that” after verbs of saying and knowing (mó ca maa n naŋ taw “he saw that it was very good” Gen 1:31).

Spelling rule

Write the tone on mi + pronoun, as the Bible does: mí, mó, má (narrative) versus mì, mò, mà (subjunctive). This is one of the rare cases where the tone mark is obligatory; see Tone.

docs.title: The imperative and the hortative
docs.text:
• 2nd person singular: the bare stem: Kɔ “go”, Cua ndu “take her” Gen 12:19.
  • 2nd person plural: la + stem: La náŋ ipúlú, la kuí Gen 1:28.
  • 1st person plural (“let us go”): n + stem: N kɔ delnun ndu coo Gen 37:20.
  • 3rd person (“let him…”): subject + stem with high tone, which the Bible often marks: Ɲɔ́ɔ́ téngá “Let there be light” Gen 1:3, Yondoo fulá “let the vegetation come forth” Gen 1:11.

Southern Kissi likewise distinguishes the imperative and the hortative by tone (Childs 1995, p. 227-231).

docs.title: “Not yet”, “already”
docs.text:
• vɔ … le “not yet”: Mɛlɛka Hala ndóò tuisi vɔ piɔɔ … le “the Lord God had not yet sent rain” Gen 2:5 (Southern Kissi wɔ̀ (Childs 1995, p. 238-239));
  • bɛɛ … le “not yet, not even”: O cii bɛɛ piɛilen tosa le “he had not yet finished speaking” Gen 24:15;
  • cii “finish” + verb expresses the completed action: Mɛɛ Hala cii baala kon tosa kpow “when God had finished his work” Gen 2:2.

1979 usage

The 1979 description gives conjugation tables by tense (durative present with tyo, habitual present, past, near and distant future, imperfect with va, imperative, conditional, subjunctive) (Keita 1979, p. 94-104). The auxiliary tyo is written co in the Bible. The tone distinctions between habitual present and past are not marked there; they still need to be described with speakers (see the open questions).

docs.title: Regional varieties
docs.text: In Guinea two main groups of varieties are distinguished (Keita 1979, p. 8-10). Speakers understand each other without difficulty: the grammar is the same, and the differences mainly concern the pronunciation of a few sounds and part of the vocabulary.

docs.title: Kpekeduei and Kisiduei
docs.text:
Group Region Features Kpekeduei (Guéckédou variety) Guéckédou prefecture; south of Kissidougou (Kondiadou) No r sound: people say l. Loanwords from Loma, Mende and Krio depending on the area. Three sub-varieties are distinguished: Kisii malowwe (west), Luannde (east) and Sayaninnde (centre). Kisiduei (Kissidougou variety) Kissidougou, Faranah The r sound exists where Kpekeduei has l; loanwords from Maninka.

Some correspondences (respelled forms) (Keita 1979, p. 8-10):

Meaning Kpekeduei Kisiduei mat valaa varaa bag bɔlɔɔ bɔrɔɔ wrapper (cloth) kolaa koraa, tafeo elephant kamaa sɛmbaa pig pewvo poovo

The handwritten annotations in the digitised copy Annotations manuscrites portées sur l'exemplaire numérisé de Keita (1979) (s.d.) add other Kissidougou variants (marked “Kdg”): doo for dioo “eat”, tyallo for kiallo “doe”, työndöö for kiöndöö “pick”, voröö for violöö “give birth” (forms quoted in the old spelling). Similar alternations between c and k from one variety to another are reported elsewhere in the Kissi area (Childs 1995, p. 30).

Rule

The Bible follows the Guéckédou variety: it writes l where Kissidougou pronounces r (kolaa, never koraa). The letter r appears in the Bible only in proper names and loanwords (Israɛl, Abraham). So write the form with l, even if you pronounce r.

The distribution of r is confirmed by the description of Southern Kissi: the North has a distinct r, whereas the South has only l, of which [r] is just a rare variant (Childs 1995, p. 10, 33, 157).

docs.title: Words whose meaning changes from one variety to another
docs.text: Some words that are common in one variety are avoided or have another meaning in the other (Keita 1979, p. 8-10); for example kundei “clod of earth” in Kissidougou, but an intimate meaning in Guéckédou. When in doubt, choose the term used in the Bible.

docs.title: Outside Guinea
docs.text:
The 1979 manual does not describe the varieties of Sierra Leone and Liberia. They are described, under the name Southern Kissi, in a grammar and a dictionary (Childs 1995) (Childs 2000), which this guide cites for comparison. A 1973 survey distinguishes three groups: Duku in Guinea, the northernmost and most divergent; Kpekedu (Guéckédou), close to the Toli and Leyi varieties of Sierra Leone; and the varieties of Liberia and Sierra Leone (Childs 1995, p. 10, 318). Guéckédou is assigned there to the Southern area. The same survey notes that stories in Duku were poorly understood by speakers of the Southern varieties (Childs 1995, p. 10).

The differences noted between North and South concern vocabulary (“write”: sɛwaa in the North, pooɲaa in the South; the Bible writes sɛva), the r sound and a few phonological rules (Childs 1995, p. 10, 318). The Bible does not always follow the forms given for the North: it writes bollen “head”, like the South, and not botteŋ (Childs 1995, p. 318).

This guide does not deal with these varieties in their own right. Speakers from these regions are invited to report the differences (see Open questions).

docs.title: Kisiei examples
docs.text:
All Kisiei words and sentences are in underlined italics. The colour and style of the underline show where the form comes from; details appear when you move the mouse (or your finger) over it.

Mark Status What it means cɛiyo Attested Every word occurs in the Kisiei Bible (BKG), apart from tones and capitals. docs.text:
• Bible: Gen 1:3 links to the verse on bible.com. The book abbreviations are the usual English ones (Gen, Exod, Matt…).
  • Keita 1979: “(Keita 1979, p. 24)” refers to the typed page of the manual; the full transcription is in the archive.
  • The other sources are listed in the bibliography.

docs.title: Boxes
docs.text:
Rule

A spelling or grammar rule to remember.

1979 usage

What the 1979 manual says when it differs from the Bible's usage. The guide follows the Bible.

Note

A remark, an exception or a clarification.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text: Translations of the examples are literal when this helps to understand the construction: words added for the English are in square brackets, and grammatical glosses in small capitals appear only in the Grammar chapter.

docs.title: Technical terms
docs.text: The guide avoids jargon as far as possible; the necessary terms (stem, noun class, referent, tone…) are explained in the glossary.

docs.title: The Kisiei language
docs.text: Kisiei (also written kissi, kisi or kisie; ISO 639-3 code kqs) is the language of the Kisia (sing. Kisinɔɔ). It is also called Northern Kissi to distinguish it from Southern Kissi, spoken in Sierra Leone and Liberia. It belongs to the Mel branch of the Atlantic languages (Niger-Congo family); its closest relatives are Sherbro and Krim in Sierra Leone, as Homburger (1941) already noted.

docs.title: Where Kisiei is spoken
docs.text:
Kisiei is spoken (Keita 1979, p. 6-8):

  • in Guinea, in the prefectures of Guéckédou (the mother tongue of about 97% of the inhabitants at the time), Kissidougou (more than two thirds) and in the south of Faranah prefecture (sub-prefectures of Bagna and Kobikoro);
  • in Sierra Leone, in the districts of Kailahun (Bouliedou, Diah, Kama) and Kono (Soa, Toli, Gbané, Lei, Mafindo);
  • in Liberia, in the Wam chiefdom, in the north of the country.

The Kissi region is an area of forest and farming; rice holds a central place there (Paulme 1954). The neighbouring languages (Maninka, Kuranko, Loma, Mende, Kono, Gbandi, Lele) have left loanwords, which differ from one variety to another (see Regional varieties).

docs.title: General features
docs.text:
What this guide describes in detail:

  • Noun classes marked by suffixes: a noun ends in a vowel or in -an, -lan, -len, etc., and this suffix shows its class and number (see Noun classes).
  • Agreement by repetition: determiners, pronouns and relatives repeat the suffix of the noun; this is what is called the alliterative structure (Keita 1979, p. 121-122) (see Agreement).
  • Stem forms and full forms: a noun followed by a determiner loses its suffix (cɛiyo “the house” → cɛi kon “that house”).
  • Verb stems that change their vowel according to tense, mood and polarity (see Stems and verb groups).
  • A tone language, with two levels (high and low), which distinguish words and tenses; the spelling marks tones only in certain cases (see Tone).
  • Subject – verb – object word order, with tense auxiliaries placed between the subject and the verb.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• How to read this guide
  • Regional varieties
  • History of writing
  • Sources and the standard

docs.title: Why the Bible is authoritative
docs.text:
A spelling is useful only if everyone writes the same way. The Kisiei Bible (BKG) is today the longest, most widely read and most carefully proofread text in the current spelling: it contains several hundred thousand words and thousands of different words. It therefore serves as the standard:

  1. When the Bible writes a word, write it the same way.
  2. When the Bible writes the same word in two ways, take the more frequent form (often the one without a tone accent; see Tone).
  3. When a word is not in the Bible, apply the rules of this guide; the form is marked Respelled until a speaker confirms it.

Biblical proper names (Abraham, Israɛl) follow the Bible's usage but do not serve as a model for Kisiei words.

docs.title: Keita's manual (1979)
docs.text:
Kisiei fondamental by Sékou Sondo Keita (1979) is a final-year thesis intended for people learning Kisiei. It describes pronunciation, noun classes, agreement, pronouns, conjugation and syntax, with exercises, dialogues and a Kisiei–French glossary of about 700 words. This guide uses it as the basic description of the grammar, bearing in mind three limitations:

  • it is written in the 1970s spelling (ty, nh, ny, è, ö), without tones;
  • it contains typing errors and a few mistakes, sometimes corrected by hand in the surviving copy;
  • some rules are simplified or do not match the Bible's usage (for example the spelling of relatives).

The digitised copy bears many handwritten annotations by later readers (translations, Kissidougou variants, corrections) Annotations manuscrites portées sur l'exemplaire numérisé de Keita (1979) (s.d.). They are cited when they shed light on a point.

docs.title: Other sources
docs.text:
Keita (1979) cites several works by the Académie des Langues and theses from the Institut polytechnique de Conakry (Tolno, Sow, Kamano, Camara, Iffono), which could not be consulted. They are listed in the bibliography for anyone who wishes to track them down.

The most complete description published since is G. Tucker Childs's grammar in English (1995), supplemented by his dictionary (2000). Childs relies mainly on the Kissi spoken in Liberia and Sierra Leone; his analyses (tones, classes, verb) are valuable, but his forms and spelling do not apply as they are to the Kisiei of Guinea. This guide cites them as a point of comparison, never as a standard.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
For each point of grammar:

  1. start from Keita's description;
  2. look for the corresponding forms in the text of the Bible with a concordance tool;
  3. keep the rule if the Bible confirms it, correct it if the Bible contradicts it, and complete it with what else the Bible shows;
  4. choose the examples from the Bible, with their reference; Keita's examples are used only when the Bible has nothing equivalent.
flowchart TD
    K["Rule described by Keita (1979)"] --> B["Search for the forms in the Bible<br>(concordance)"]
    B --> Q{"What does the Bible show?"}
    Q -- "it confirms the rule" --> G["Keep the rule"]
    Q -- "it contradicts it" --> C["Correct the rule"]
    Q -- "it shows more" --> P["Complete the rule"]
    G --> E["Examples taken from the Bible,<br>with their reference"]
    C --> E
    P --> E
    CH["Childs (1995, 2000):<br>comparison with Southern Kissi"] -.-> Q
The method followed for each point of grammar. The Bible decides; Childs serves for comparison.

Points that neither source can settle are collected in the open questions.

docs.title: The spelling of the 1970s
docs.text:
After Guinea's independence, the national languages were taught from the Cultural Revolution of 1968 onwards; the Académie des Langues in Conakry published Principes d'orthographe et de segmentation (principles of spelling and word division) for Kisiei Académie des Langues (s.d.). Keita's manual (1979) follows this spelling. It is based on the Latin alphabet of the French typewriter and renders the sounds specific to Kisiei with letter groups and accented vowels:

Sound 1970s spelling Example (1979) [c] (palatal “ch”) ty tyuaa “child” [ŋ] nh nhuèènu “five” [ɲ] ny nyumndan “night” [ɛ] (open e) è dènè [ɔ] (open o) ö söö “chicken”

This spelling does not mark tones.

docs.title: The current spelling
docs.text:
The current spelling replaces these groups with single letters from the African reference alphabet: c, ŋ, ɲ, ɛ, ɔ Nouvelle orthographe kissi (tableau de correspondances) (s.d.). The correspondence sheet kept in the archive also gives “mb = nb”; the Bible, however, always writes mb (pɔmbɔɔ, kumbu), and this is the usage the guide follows.

The Kisiei Bible (BKG) is the major text published in this spelling. It adds practices that the correspondence sheet does not mention:

  • ŋ at the end of a stem, including before suffixes in -nd-: lɛŋnden “country” (1979: lènnden), naŋ “good” (1979: nan);
  • tones, marked by accents on certain words only (Ɲɔ́ɔ́ téngá Gen 1:3);
  • the hyphen, which attaches relatives and class markers at the end of a clause (fula-o, nin-nda) and joins compound and reduplicated words (ɲɛ-ɲɛ, taw-taw);
  • « » quotation marks for reported speech.

The Spelling chapter describes these rules, and the correspondence table helps to rewrite a 1979 text in the current spelling.

docs.title: The letters
docs.text:
The Kisiei alphabet has 26 letters. The letters specific to Kisiei are ɛ, ɔ, ŋ and ɲ; the letters j, q, x and z are not used (they do not appear even once in the Bible (BKG)).

Lower case Capital Proposed name Example Meaning a A a kolaa wrapper (cloth) b B be bɛndoo big c C ce cɛiyo house d D de diolan name e E e pelei foot ɛ Ɛ ɛ lɛŋnden country, land f F fe fuɲaa father g G ge tenga shine, be bright h H he hala God i I i pilɛ one k K ke kalaa mother l L le lɛŋ (on the) ground, soil m M me mɛnndan water n N ne naŋ good ŋ Ŋ ŋe ŋuɛɛnu five ɲ Ɲ ɲe ɲumndan night, darkness o O o yɔmndo tree ɔ Ɔ ɔ pɔmbɔɔ small, younger p P pe pee river r R re Abraham (proper name) s S se sɛbɛ book, letter t T te tiɔn two u U u cuaa child v V ve vana person w W we taw much, many y Y ye yáá three

The letter names follow the usage described in 1979 (Keita 1979, p. 14): each consonant is pronounced followed by a short e (be, de, fe…) and not the French way (bé, dé, èf…).

docs.title: Double letters
docs.text:
Several sounds are written with two letters. These are not sequences of two sounds, but a single consonant:

Group Sound Example Meaning kp [k͡p] labial-velar stop kpemaa covenant gb [ɡ͡b] labial-velar stop langbanɔɔ adult man, elder mb [ᵐb] prenasalised pɔmbɔɔ small nd [ⁿd] prenasalised ndu him, her ng [ᵑɡ] prenasalised tenga shine ll [lː] long l hangullo heat

The prenasalised consonants and kp are also analysed as single consonants in Southern Kissi (Childs 1995, p. 24, 30-31). The ll, on the other hand, is described there as two ls belonging to two syllables (Childs 1995, p. 151) (see Consonants).

Long vowels (aa, ee, ɛɛ, ii, oo, ɔɔ, uu) are described on the Vowels page.

docs.title: Letters with a restricted position
docs.text:
Some letters appear only in certain positions in the word:

  • g appears only in ng and gb; no Kisiei word begins with g. In Southern Kissi, too, g does not exist on its own: an initial g in a loanword becomes k or ng there (Childs 1995, p. 25, 30).
  • w is written only after a vowel, at the end of a syllable: taw, kpow, nawvo. No word begins with w.
  • r appears only in proper names and loanwords: Abraham, rɛsɛn “grape”. Some Northern varieties pronounce r in ordinary Kisiei words, but the Bible writes l in them (see Regional varieties).
  • ŋ is found mainly at the end of a stem (naŋ, lɛŋ) and before n (lɛŋnden); at the beginning of a word it appears only in a few words, including the numbers ŋuɛɛnu “five” and ŋɔmpum “six”.

docs.title: Alphabetical order
docs.text:
For sorting words (glossaries, indexes), the following order is proposed, in which each letter specific to Kisiei follows the closest Latin letter:

a b c d e ɛ f g h i k l m n ŋ ɲ o ɔ p r s t u v w y

The groups kp, gb, mb, nd, ng are sorted under their first letter (kpemaa under k). Tone accents are ignored in sorting.

Note

This order is a proposal of this guide; neither the 1979 manual nor the Bible gives one. See the open questions.

docs.title: Simple consonants
docs.text:
Letter Pronunciation Example Meaning b as in bed bala hands c [c], between t and ch, like t-y in got you said quickly cuaa child d as in day diolan name f as in fun fula go out h always pronounced, as in English house hun come k as in skin, without a puff of air kalaa mother l as in let; ll is a long l, as in tall lamp lɛŋ / kɔllo ground / heart m as in man mɛnndan water n as in net nin in ŋ ng of English sing ŋuɛɛnu five ɲ ny of canyon ɲɛ thing p as in spin, without a puff of air pee river s always hissing, even between two vowels sɔɔn words t as in stop, without a puff of air tiɔn two v as in van vana person w w of watt, only after a vowel taw much, many y y of yes yáá three

In Southern Kissi, b and d are implosive and occur mainly at the beginning of words (Childs 1995, p. 27); c there varies between [tʃ] and an almost velar articulation (Childs 1995, p. 31).

w and y are classed as semivowels (Keita 1979, p. 14): y begins syllables (yɔmndo “tree”), whereas w only ends them (nawvo “cow” is divided naw-vo). In Southern Kissi, [w] also begins syllables and is pronounced [v] before i, e and often a (Childs 1995, p. 33-36); the Bible then writes v: vana “person” corresponds to Southern Kissi wànà (Childs 1995, p. 199).

docs.title: The sounds c, ŋ, ɲ
docs.text:
Rule

Sound Write No longer write (1979) [c] c: cuaa, cɛiyo ty: tyuaa, tyièiyo [ŋ] ŋ: ŋuɛɛnu, naŋ nh: nhuèènu [ɲ] ɲ: ɲɛ, ɲumndan ny: nyè, nyumndan

The sequences ny and nh are now written only when n and y (or h) belong to two different syllables, which is rare (Bɛnyamɛn “Benjamin”).

docs.title: Labial-velar consonants: kp, gb
docs.text:
kp and gb are pronounced by closing the back of the mouth (as for k, g) and the lips (as for p, b) at the same time. They are single consonants, not sequences k + p.

  • kp occurs at the beginning and in the middle of words: kpemaa “covenant”, kpow “all”, kpede “all together”.
  • gb occurs only in the middle of words, after a nasal vowel (Keita 1979, p. 15): langbanɔɔ “adult man”, kpingbi. In the Bible, gb always follows n, m or ŋ. In Southern Kissi, [gb] is described as the form kp takes after a nasal (Childs 1995, p. 28, 31).

docs.title: Prenasalised consonants: mb, nd, ng
docs.text:
These consonants begin with a short nasal resonance.

  • mb: pɔmbɔɔ, kumbu, pembei.
  • nd: very frequent, especially in pronouns and class suffixes: ndu “him”, nda “them”, yɔmndo, mɛnndan.
  • ng: tenga “shine”, kpengii “side, direction”.

The correspondence sheet

The “new spelling” sheet in the archive Nouvelle orthographe kissi (tableau de correspondances) (s.d.) says “mb = nb”. The Bible never writes nb and keeps mb (pɔmbɔɔ, tɛɛmbuu): write mb.

docs.title: n and ŋ
docs.text:
At the end of a stem, Kisiei distinguishes n and ŋ: nan “pull” / naŋ “good”. The old spelling wrote both as n; the Bible (BKG) writes ŋ where [ŋ] is pronounced:

  • at the end of a word: naŋ, lɛŋ, baŋ, yɔŋ;
  • before a suffix that begins with n: the stem keeps its ŋ, and the suffix is added after it. So write ŋn where 1979 wrote nn:
Stem Full form (Bible) Old spelling lɛŋ lɛŋnden “country” lènnden yɔŋ yɔŋnun “become” yönnun — ciŋnde “tooth” tyinnde — tɔŋndo “word, command” tönndo

On the other hand, when the stem ends in n, write nn: mɛnndan “water” (stem mɛn-), vannda “people” (stem van-).

In Southern Kissi, n never occurs at the end of a syllable: the final nasal there is always [ŋ] (or m), and it becomes n when a suffix beginning with a vowel is added (Childs 1995, p. 22-24). The Bible, which distinguishes final -n and -ŋ (hun “come” / naŋ “good”), remains the reference.

How to choose

To know whether to write nn or ŋn, look at the short form of the word: if it ends in ŋ (lɛŋ), the long form is written with ŋn (lɛŋnden). When in doubt, check in the Bible or in the lexicon.

Before g, simply write ng, never ŋg: tenga, kpengii.

docs.title: The long consonant ll
docs.text: l can be long; it is then written ll. The first l closes a syllable, the second opens the next one (Keita 1979, p. 16): kɔllo kɔl-lo “heart”, hangullo han-gul-lo “heat”, bolle bol-le “head, top”. ll appears mainly when a suffix beginning with l is added to a stem ending in l: vallo “(the) work”, dimullo “say to”. In Southern Kissi, a suffix beginning with a vowel likewise takes an l after a stem in l (Childs 1995, p. 151). Before a suffix in l, the second l there often becomes t (Childs 1995, p. 155-156); the Bible also has this lt in some words (hɔlten “eye”, bóltan “heads”), but not in others (bollen “head”).

docs.title: The apostrophe: n'
docs.text: Before a consonant, an n that forms a syllable on its own is written n' and attached to the following word: n'van tɔ́ “ten people” Gen 42:3, n'rɛsɛnndo “vine”. This is a nasal prefix; its meaning is described in the Grammar chapter.

docs.title: Spelling
docs.text: This chapter describes the current spelling of Kisiei as practised in the Bible (BKG). The rules are drawn from the usage observed in that text (more than 300,000 words) and compared with the 1979 description of the sounds (Keita 1979, p. 11-19).

docs.title: The essentials in ten rules
docs.text:
Basic rules

  1. The alphabet has 26 letters: a b c d e ɛ f g h i k l m n ŋ ɲ o ɔ p r s t u v w y. The letters j q x z are not used (Alphabet).
  2. There are seven vowels: a e ɛ i o ɔ u. A long vowel is written doubled: kolaa, pɔmbɔɔ (Vowels).
  3. The sounds [c], [ŋ], [ɲ] are written c, ŋ, ɲ — never ty, nh, ny as in 1979 (Consonants).
  4. kp and gb are single consonants; mb, nd, ng represent prenasalised consonants (kpemaa, pɔmbɔɔ, ndu).
  5. ŋ is written at the end of a stem, even before a suffix in -nd-: naŋ, lɛŋnden; before g, write ng: tenga.
  6. Tones are marked only on certain words: grammatical words whose tone changes the meaning (mí / mì) and a few words that would otherwise be confused (Tone).
  7. Write a noun in its full form when it stands alone (cɛiyo) and in its stem form before a determiner (cɛi kon) (Word division).
  8. The hyphen attaches a relative or a class marker to the preceding word at the end of a clause (fula-o), and joins compounds and reduplicated words (ɲɛ-ɲɛ, taw-taw).
  9. Punctuation is as in French, with the quotation marks « » and ‹ › (Punctuation and capitals).
  10. Write l even in the varieties that pronounce r; r is reserved for proper names and loanwords (Proper names and loanwords).

docs.text:

docs.title: Kissi proper names
docs.text:
Kissi first names and surnames are written with the Kisiei alphabet like other words. The names given according to birth order, very frequent in the examples of the 1979 manual (Keita 1979) — Tamba, Saa, Fallo, Faya, Kumba, Sia, Finda, Teeva… — contain no special letter and do not change.

For a name that contained ty, nh, ny, è, ö in the old spelling, apply the same correspondences as for other words (see From the old to the new spelling). In official documents (civil registers, identity cards), the name may keep the French spelling already in use; it is then quoted as it is, without being respelled.

docs.title: Foreign proper names
docs.text:
The Bible (BKG) adapts biblical names to the Kisiei alphabet, but keeps letters that do not exist in ordinary Kisiei words, in particular r:

Name (French) In Kisiei (Bible) Abraham Abraham Israël Israɛl Égypte Esipte Jérusalem Yerusalɛm Benjamin Bɛnyamɛn

Note that:

  • French è becomes ɛ (Israɛl);
  • j becomes y (Yerusalɛm, Bɛnyamɛn);
  • z and soft g are replaced by Kisiei sounds (Esipte for Égypte).

Names of peoples take Kisiei class suffixes: Israɛlla “the Israelites”, Aarɔn-nda “those of Aaron”.

docs.title: Loanwords
docs.text:
Kisiei has borrowed words from Maninka, French, English and Krio. Once integrated, a loanword is written with the Kisiei alphabet and takes a class suffix like a Kisiei word:

sɛbɛ “book, letter” (from Maninka), volion “money”, rɛsɛn “grape” (from French), kafo “festival, meeting”.

In Southern Kissi, a loanword adapts to the Kissi syllable: a consonant cluster is broken up by a vowel, and a word that would begin with a vowel often receives an h; Hala “God” thus comes from Arabic Allah (Childs 1995, p. 64-65). Loanwords there mostly enter class o in the singular and la in the plural (Childs 1995, p. 163). Biblical proper names, by contrast, keep their consonant clusters (Israɛl, Esipte).

Rule

  • An integrated loanword is written in Kisiei spelling: do not use é, è, ou or ch in it (rɛsɛn, not raisin).
  • r may be kept in a loanword where it is pronounced (rɛsɛn).
  • A non-integrated foreign word (brand name, quotation) is put in italics and keeps its original spelling.

The varieties differ precisely in their loanwords: Kisiduei borrows from Maninka, Kpekeduei from Loma, Mende and Krio (Keita 1979, p. 8-10) (see Regional varieties). In a text intended for everyone, prefer the common Kisiei word when there is one.

docs.title: From the old to the new spelling
docs.text: Kisiei texts from the 1970s and 1980s, including Keita's manual (1979), are written in the old spelling. This page explains how to read them and rewrite them.

docs.title: Basic correspondences
docs.text:
These are the correspondences on the “new spelling” sheet Nouvelle orthographe kissi (tableau de correspondances) (s.d.), checked against the Bible (BKG):

Old New Old example New example Meaning ty c tyuaa cuaa child nh ŋ nhuèènu ŋuɛɛnu five ny ɲ nyumndan ɲumndan night è ɛ Lènnden → lɛŋnden country ö ɔ pomböö pɔmbɔɔ small, younger mb mb (unchanged) tyuaamböö cuaambɔɔ child

For capitals: Ty → C, Nh → Ŋ, Ny → Ɲ, È → Ɛ, Ö → Ɔ.

mb = nb?

The correspondence sheet says “mb = nb”. The Bible never writes nb: keep mb.

docs.title: What the basic correspondences cannot capture
docs.text: Applying only the table above to the roughly 700 words of the glossary and verb list of the 1979 manual, about four words in ten are found unchanged in the Bible. For the others, either the word does not appear in the Bible (vocabulary of daily life, illnesses, tools…), or the Bible's spelling differs on one of the following points.

docs.title: 1. ŋ at the end of a stem
docs.text:
The old spelling wrote n for both [n] and [ŋ] at the end of a syllable. The Bible distinguishes them:

1979 Bible Meaning Lènnden lɛŋnden country, land Tyinnde ciŋnde tooth Tyannda caŋnda hips Tinndo tiŋndo interval, space (1979: “island” (Keita 1979, p. 155)) Dièn diɛŋ the day after tomorrow nan “good” naŋ good

There is no mechanical rule: you need to know whether the stem ends in [n] or [ŋ] (see Consonants). When in doubt, look the word up in the Bible or in the lexicon of this guide.

docs.title: 2. Tones
docs.text: The old spelling did not mark tones. When rewriting, add accents only where the Bible puts them: on mí/mì, mó/mò, má/mà and a few other words (see Tone).

docs.title: 3. Relatives and referents
docs.text: The 1979 spelling writes relatives as separate words (Domaa n pendu vo sèsa) (Keita 1979, p. 88-89). The Bible attaches the referent to the last word of the phrase with a hyphen (kɔngɔ vesɛi fula-o). The description of Southern Kissi likewise analyses this marker as a suffix placed at the end of the relative clause (Childs 1995, p. 285-286). See Word division.

docs.title: 4. Errors and variants in the manual
docs.text: The typed manual contains typing errors and some forms specific to the author's variety. Before rewriting a word from 1979, it is best to check that it is not garbled (the transcription flags doubtful passages).

docs.title: Method for rewriting an old text
docs.text:
1. Replace ty, nh, ny, è, ö with c, ŋ, ɲ, ɛ, ɔ (without touching the French).
  2. Look up each word in the Bible or in the lexicon; if it is there, take that form (watch out for n / ŋ and vowel length).
  3. Rewrite the relatives with the hyphen.
  4. Add tone accents on the small words that carry them.
  5. Mark the words you have not found as “to be confirmed”.
flowchart TD
